title: Pooled Calendar Reporters for Limited-Scope Family Lawyers
one_liner: One physically present reporter sits an entire family-court calendar and sells the record by the matter, about $110 per 15-minute hearing, so each lawyer pays roughly 75% less than a half-day pro tem while the reporter earns more than a normal pro tem day.
customer: Wedge: limited-scope (unbundled) and solo family-law attorneys who appear on DVRO, custody and support calendars in ONE high-volume California courthouse, plus the non-indigent 'missing middle' litigants they represent, who fail the fee-waiver test but cannot spend $450 on a record. Not indigent litigants (the FVAP ruling moves them to a court-paid record) and not the court.
problem: About 7 in 10 civil, family and probate hearings in California have no verbatim record, and appeals of custody and restraining-order rulings fail without one. Courts tell litigants to 'arrange your own' reporter, but a private pro tem costs $450-500 for a half day, and no one pays that for a 12-minute item. The parent's fix (remote reporters dialing in) is barred by Gov. Code 69959 and by the 69959.5 pilot limits, so it cannot launch as written. The parent also has no proof that anyone will pay $95, and the ruling shrinks the legal-aid segment.
solution: Drop remote reporting and prediction. A reporter is physically in the department for the whole morning or afternoon calendar, which is the lawful 'bring your own reporter' route. Attorneys book a matter slot the day before at $110 for up to 15 minutes, plus a per-page certified transcript (about $8/page) only if they order one. Booking is all-or-nothing, like a crowdfund: the reporter goes only if at least 6-8 matters are booked by 5pm the day before, otherwise everyone is refunded. That kills the dead-time problem without any duration model. Each party gets only its own matter's transcript, and other matters on the reporter's notes are never released. Cross-department hopping and duration prediction come later, once the manual logs give real data. Unit economics (assumptions to test): 2 sessions/day x 8 matters x $110 = $1,760 gross. The reporter keeps about 60% ($1,056) versus $900-1,000 for two half-day pro tem bookings, and the company keeps about $700 per reporter-day before ops.
why_now: FVAP v. Superior Court (Aug 10, 2026) put the 70% no-record gap in every family lawyer's inbox. It also makes courts serve only indigent litigants, which leaves a large paying middle. Courts are already telling family litigants in writing to arrange their own reporter. The reporter shortage (about 5,500 short by 2030) means freelancers can choose better-paying days, so a higher-yield day is a real recruiting pitch.
revenue_model: $110 per matter slot for up to 15 minutes, $8/page for certified transcripts, and prepaid 5-packs ($500) for cash up front. The reporter keeps about 60% of slot fees, the platform keeps about 40% (about 35% gross margin after the payment and ops costs of a services business). Year-2 add-ons: a subscription for attorneys who book 8+ hearings a month, and referral-funded 'record scholarships' from DV appellate nonprofits.
non_obvious_insight: Once the first attorney in a department triggers the reporter's presence, every other matter that day costs roughly nothing extra, so the price can fall 75% while the reporter's day pay rises. Limited-scope attorneys are the right buyer because they bill flat per hearing and can pass the record fee through as an itemized line, while a full-service litigator does not think of the record as a per-hearing line item. The tipping-point booking rule replaces the prediction model the parent needed.
first_30_days: Week 1: one-week legal check with a court-reporter licensing attorney and the clerks of the 2 target departments (private pro tem in the room, multiple parties sharing one reporter, closed-hearing rules, and any court-reporting-firm registration). Weeks 1-2: pick the single biggest family courthouse in one county, recruit 3 physically local pro tem reporters, and pre-sell 5-packs to 15 limited-scope attorneys from the family-law bar and unbundled-services listservs. Weeks 3-4: run the first 10 calendars with a Google Sheet, Stripe links and a group text, using the booking threshold, and log booked-matter density and actual call order per department. Offer FVAP and one DV appellate nonprofit free slots for cases they flag as appeal-bound.
lineage: mutation of I0248 ('Fifteen-Minute Court Reporting for Family Law Hearings'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Steno (Steno Agency Inc.), DirectDep, StenoScout, Incumbent agencies (Veritext, Esquire, Combs Reporting, Coalition Court Reporters). White space: Nobody offers flat-fee coverage of 15-minute California family-law hearings. That is because the core mechanic, private reporters dialing in from anywhere, is currently barred. Gov. Code 69959 says 'Remote court reporting shall not be used by courts to make the record of any court proceedings' and defines it as a stenographer not present in the courtroom (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959/). The only exception, Gov. Code 69959.5, allows remote reporting only by 'full-time official reporters ... employed by the participating superior court', physically in a court facility, in 13 pilot counties, capped at 10-20% of reporters (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959-5/). San Diego's court page states 'the court is prohibited by law from allowing remote court reporting for any court proceeding' (https://sdcourt.ca.gov/sdcourt/generalinformation/resourcelists/courtreporterinformation). The idea's claim that AB 3013 'opened remote reporting' to a private platform is wrong. Unserved and still legal: (1) physical-presence short-hearing coverage, where one pro tem covers several departments in the same courthouse using calendar-based duration prediction, and no vendor markets a per-hearing SKU; (2) a scheduling and utilization layer sold to courts to fill pro tem and official reporter slots, aimed at hiring and retention (the ruling names 'pro tem reporters paid by the court' as a compliance route, and court reporter counsel is calling on courts to lift hiring freezes); (3) fast certified transcripts of court electronic recordings for attorneys who need appellate-grade records. The white space is real but is a legal-regime bet on remote reporting being opened to private reporters, plus a narrow physical-hopping wedge. It is not a software-only wedge. Court reporter unions opposed AB 3013 and are a political headwind. | How this version avoids them: Steno, DirectDep, StenoScout and the agencies (Veritext, Esquire and others) sell a whole appearance to one buyer, mostly depositions, so every buyer pays the full minimum, and their half-day minimum is structural. We sell the matter, split one appearance across many paying parties, and stay lawful without remote reporting. The AB 3013 pilot covers only court-employed reporters in a court facility, capped at 10-20% of reporters in 13 counties. We serve paying litigants in any county and do not compete for the court-employed slots. eScribers and Verbit transcribe recordings, which fits the court's indigent fallback but not an attorney who wants a stenographic record, live and immediate. The moat, if the wedge works, is proprietary calendar density and call-order data per department, and reporter loyalty from the higher day yield, which points to a cornered-resource advantage in one courthouse before any scale.

title: Mzee's Testament: Family Land Councils Before Death
one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of untangling the dead man's land after the funeral, hold a video-witnessed Family Land Council this December while the parent is alive and every heir is home, lock it into a will, family agreement, capacity certificate and time-locked vault, and grow the format into a registry of family land intent.
customer: Diaspora and urban children (30-55) with living rural parents aged 65-90 who hold unsubdivided family land. The child pays in September-November for a December council, but the parent is the legal client of the partner advocate. Later payers are SACCOs, lenders and insurers who buy verified family land plans (with family consent), and churches and clan associations as channels.
problem: After death, succession takes 1-3 years, is contested and costs heirs dearly (parent's figures). Every year of delay means heirs die, feuds harden, and evidence disappears. Children abroad only get all siblings into one compound at Christmas. Parents avoid 'death talk' and fear that gifting land makes them dependants. Where informal wills exist they are often unwitnessed or challenged for lack of capacity or undue influence, and daughters and second households are frequently excluded by custom, which produces litigation later. No one sells a cheap, provable record of what the parent actually wanted, agreed by all children while the parent can still speak.
solution: 'Family Land Council': a one-day facilitated event at the family home in the 20 Dec to 5 Jan window, prepared in October-November by WhatsApp intake, an official title search, a heir list including second households and a parcel sketch. On the day a team of three attends: a facilitator, a partner advocate who acts for the parent and first meets the parent alone, and a videographer, plus a clinician's capacity assessment on site or the same week. Outputs: (1) the parent's recorded, parent-alone statement of wishes; (2) a Family Land Agreement signed by all adult children in person or by video (allocation, parent's lifetime use and residence, burial ground, provision for daughters and widows); (3) a properly witnessed will drafted by the advocate; (4) an encrypted Family Land Vault holding video, documents and a machine-readable Family Land Plan, released to named heirs only when a death certificate is uploaded and two heirs confirm. Optional track: transfer by gift or subdivision with the parent's use protected, through surveyor, Land Control Board consent and registry, which skips the court queue entirely. The exact legal structure (gift versus will, consent requirements, stamp duty treatment) must be confirmed with Kenyan counsel.
why_now: December 2026 is about ten weeks away and diaspora flights are booked in October-November, so the product's launch window is literal. The allottee generation is 65-90 now: each year removes some of the people whose testimony is the whole point. LLMs, phone video and e-signature make an evidence pack cheap, and drafting is commoditising (Wakili-Intel, July 2026) while witnessing, capacity evidence and convening a family are not. Remittances of roughly US$5bn a year (parent's figure, verify) show families already pay to 'sort out the land' from abroad. This would have worked in 2019 only as a boutique law-firm service; the cost of running councils at scale with intake, video and vault software is new.
revenue_model: Council package: KES 40k service fee (about US$310) for pre-work, facilitation, video and capacity evidence and vault setup, pilot price KES 25k. The advocate's will and agreement drafting (KES 15-25k, assumption) is billed directly by the advocate to the parent as client, and the clinician's fee is passed through at cost. Vault subscription KES 3k a year per family (annual refresh video on the parent's birthday, updates for births, marriages and deaths), target 60% attach. Gift or subdivision track: KES 20k service fee on top of surveyor, Land Control Board and registry costs at cost. Later B2B: per-verified-plan fees from SACCOs, lenders and insurers, with consent. Year one aim: 50-60 councils, about KES 2M revenue at roughly 55% gross margin (cost about KES 14-18k per council), validating the model rather than making money. Scale-up: church and clan chapters delivering 500+ councils per December.
non_obvious_insight: The paying child is the likeliest future litigant, so the product only works if the parent is the client: parent alone on tape, an independent advocate, a capacity certificate and a cooling-off period. That evidence can only be produced while the parent is alive, which is why no post-death service, however good, can replace it. December is the one moment all 8-20 heirs are physically together and emotionally invested, so the coordination problem that costs a year after death costs a day before it. The inversion also turns a one-off dead-paperwork job into a living, recurring relationship (vault refresh, births and deaths) whose data compounds into a standard-setting registry of family land intent.
first_30_days: October: recruit two advocates who do wills and agree a parent-as-client engagement letter, and one clinician for capacity assessments. Run a dry-run council for a friendly family (Murang'a or Kakamega) to time the day and script the parent-alone interview. Launch a landing page and WhatsApp booking with 30 December slots at the KES 25k pilot price and a 30% M-Pesa deposit, sold through diaspora Facebook and WhatsApp groups, church and alumni networks, with a free 'Family Land Map' quiz as lead magnet. Recruit and train four facilitators (paralegals, community mobilisers, retired chief's assistants). Targets: 15 paid slots by 30 October and 30 by end of November. The riskiest assumption is that parents agree, so measure the parent-consent rate among families whose child pays (target above 60%).
lineage: mutation of I0474 ('Dead Capital: Succession Kits for Diaspora Families'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Luru (open-source 'Kenya's Digital Succession Copilot'), Wakili-Intel (AI drafting copilot for Kenyan advocates), Unclaimed Financial Assets Authority (UFAA), Ardhisasa (Ministry of Lands digital land registry). White space: Provisional, because the web search budget hit its 200-call cap before any search returned results. My evidence comes only from direct page fetches and GitHub repo searches. I found no funded startup, product or open-source project that combines (a) diaspora-paid flat-fee intake, (b) heir mapping across Kenyan name variants, (c) field-agent collection of chief's letters and thumbprint or video consent from 8-20 relatives, and (d) hand-off to partner advocates. The software pieces (family tree, readiness score, drafting copilots) exist only as zero-star hobby repos. Government platforms (Ardhisasa, court e-filing, UFAA) cover filing and claiming but not multi-heir coordination. UFAA's beneficiary claim rule makes succession a prerequisite for claiming a dead person's unclaimed assets, so a succession-first product that unlocks those assets has a logical hook. The unserved wedge is the coordination and evidence-gathering layer sold to the paying sibling abroad. It is still unproven whether ordinary advocates or land-buying-company agents already do this informally, because I could not search for them. | How this version avoids them: Advocates who draft wills (the direct competitor) sell one document to one client in an office; the council sells a convened, witnessed, family-wide process and evidence pack, with the advocate as paid partner and no fee split. Luru scores post-death readiness and Wakili-Intel drafts pleadings for advocates, both software, both after death, neither with field or convening capability. UFAA is a post-death channel; Ardhisasa and court e-filing are bypassed on the gift track and used on the succession track. Incumbents do not respond because advocates earn more from contested post-death matters and courts, the Public Trustee and funeral insurers do not run family meetings. The main threat is a government wills registry, which the format, vault and process still complement. Defensibility: data on family plans accepted by chiefs, SACCOs and lenders (network economies, cornered resource) and process power in running parent-safe councils.

title: Coder-Signed Reasonable-Value Reports for Injury Defense
one_liner: A 48-hour, coder-certified benchmark report that tells defense lawyers and auto carriers what a letter-of-protection medical bill is actually worth.
customer: Insurance defense law firms and auto-carrier litigation/SIU units handling bodily-injury claims in tort-reform states (Florida, Georgia, Texas, Louisiana first). Volume firms pay per report. Carriers pay monthly.
problem: Plaintiff-side injury cases increasingly rest on treatment provided under letters of protection (LOP), where the provider is paid from the settlement and bills at a private rate card. Defense lawyers have to show what the care is really worth. Today that means a $3-5k billing expert, a slow turnaround, and a fight over methodology. Most claims examiners cannot read a CMS-1500 or UB-04, so inflated bills mostly get paid or settled at face value.
solution: Intake the itemized bill and records. Map every line to CPT/HCPCS and revenue codes and flag unbundling (e.g. 99215-25 plus separate injection administration, physician-owned ASC facility fees stacked on the professional fee, stacked imaging reads). Benchmark each line against Medicare multiples, hospital-posted commercial negotiated rates from price-transparency files, and local percentiles. The output is a Daubert-hardened PDF signed by a certified coder (CPC/CCS) with an optional expert declaration or testimony upsell. It is a methodology plus a template, so the marginal cost per report is about an hour of coder time.
why_now: Florida's 2023 tort reform made LOP arrangements discoverable and admitted evidence of amounts actually paid. Georgia's 2025 tort reform pushed similar rules, and other states are copying. Hospital price-transparency rules that took full effect in 2026 now require actual payment amounts where rates are percentages or algorithms, so a defensible local benchmark exists for the first time.
revenue_model: $295-$695 per report. Expert declaration or testimony at $1,500-$3,500. $2-5k/month subscriptions for carriers and volume firms with a report quota. Gross margin is high because coders are paid per report as contractors.
non_obvious_insight: Inside a hospital, chargemaster prices are understood to be fiction, and every biller knows what things really get paid. Injury lawyers have been arguing about 'reasonable value' without that insider map. Certified coders also know the tells of bills built for litigation rather than payment: modifier-25 patterns, unbundled facility fees, and E/M levels that no insurer would ever pay. The market is starved of people credentialed and willing to say so on paper. The moat is a coder bench plus a methodology that survives cross-examination, not software.
first_30_days: Recruit 3-5 CPC/CCS coders (ex-hospital, remote, contractors) and one defense-attorney advisor to review the methodology memo. Build the report template from the free Medicare fee schedules plus a few metro-area price-transparency files. Cold-email about 100 Florida and Georgia defense firms and claims managers, and offer 5 free reports on live cases in exchange for a methodology review and a testimonial. Convert the first 3-5 to $349 per report, then price the expert declaration as an add-on.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Enlyte (Mitchell/Genex) Demand Package Review and Bodily Injury Integrated Solutions, FAIR Health, EvenUp, Turquoise Health. White space: Caveat: the WebSearch budget hit its cap (200 of 200) before I could run the planned searches on startups, Crunchbase, Product Hunt and forums. This verdict rests on direct page fetches only. Treat 'gap' as provisional. Before building, someone should spend an hour on the searches I could not run: 'letter of protection medical bill review', 'reasonable value expert Florida LOP', and Crunchbase/YC for 'LOP' or 'defense medical bill'.

What I could confirm: no vendor I could reach sells a fixed-fee (about $300-700), fast-turnaround, coder-certified report with an optional declaration or testimony upsell aimed at LOP reasonable value. The nearest product is Enlyte's Demand Package Review. It is a carrier-side workflow product with nurse and analyst review at 3-4 to 10 days. It shows no coder signature, no LOP framing and no testimony. It also lacks the piece defense lawyers need most, which is a signed opinion that survives cross-examination. Data companies (FAIR Health, Turquoise) sell inputs, not signed opinions. EvenUp is plaintiff-side.

Specific white space: (1) small and mid-size defense firms and panel counsel who can't justify a $3-5k expert on a $30-100k claim. (2) Coder-signed output that holds up under cross-examination, tied to the LOP disclosure record. (3) States without a statutory benchmark, where reasonable value is contested.

Two weaknesses in the pitch. (a) Florida is partly commoditized by statute. Fla. Stat. 768.0427 (https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0768/Sections/0768.0427.html) already makes evidence of what was actually paid, or 120% of Medicare (170% of Medicaid where there is no Medicare rate), the benchmark for uninsured claimants. The fetched summary does not settle whether that applies to LOP treatment, so check the statute text. A large part of the Florida 'report' is therefore a Medicare-multiple calculation from free CMS files, which a claims shop or existing vendor could copy quickly. (b) The hospital price-transparency 'why now' is weaker than the idea claims. CMS says enforcement of the new rules starts April 1, 2026 (https://www.cms.gov/priorities/key-initiatives/hospital-price-transparency). But LOP care is mostly delivered by chiropractors, pain clinics, orthopedic groups and physician-owned ASCs, not hospitals. I inferred that from how LOP cases usually work and did not verify it. The defensible professional-fee benchmarks would come from Medicare multiples, payer transparency-in-coverage files or licensed data, not hospital files.

title: Recall Drills: State QC Findings Become Worker Training
one_liner: A recall-notice system for SNAP errors: every finding from a state's own QC review and every H.R.1 rule change becomes a dollar-tagged synthetic drill within 14 days, delivered through the state's CQI field staff to new hires in its highest-error counties, with an audit trail for corrective-action plans.
customer: Wedge: North Carolina's SNAP continuous-quality-improvement (CQI) unit. Its staff are former county workers who visit each of the 100 county departments monthly, plus the counties the state has already flagged as high-error. NC's 6.69% rate sits 0.69 points above the 6% cliff, and the parent research puts crossing it at about $140M a year. Payer: the state SNAP director's training/CQI line. Users: CQI specialists and county supervisors. Next states: Louisiana (7.61%) and any state within about 1.5 points of a 6/8/10% tier line.
problem: QC findings reach workers months after the case action, as webinars and memos. H.R.1 rule churn (work-requirement, noncitizen and utility-allowance changes) creates fresh errors faster than classroom training absorbs them. New hires learn on live caseloads, and Kansas cites turnover as an error driver. Counties are told 'documenting, documenting, documenting' but have no per-worker evidence trail. A handful of CQI staff cannot be in 100 counties every day.
solution: Three pieces. (1) An error-to-drill pipeline: CQI staff upload a QC finding at element level (stacked shelter deduction after a rent change, biweekly pay-stub conversion, household member who left). Within 14 days we return a synthetic twin case, scored with PolicyEngine as the oracle and hand-checked against the state manual, and push it to the assigned counties. (2) A 30-day new-hire certification track over the top three error elements, with pre/post scores and time-to-competency. (3) A CQI console with per-county and per-worker error-type heatmaps and a one-click 'CAP evidence packet' PDF (assigned, completed, score trend) that counties attach to corrective-action documentation. Drills test the input and verification decisions workers actually make (what to verify, which income to budget, which old entry to close), not the arithmetic the eligibility system already does.
why_now: The FY2027 QC sample year opens Oct 1, 2026. It is the first year measured under the new rules and it sets the FY2030 cost share (FY2029 and later use the rate from three fiscal years earlier). FY2028 exposure is effectively locked to the state's better of FY2025 or FY2026, so the next lever is FY2027 onward. The 75% state/local admin cost share also starts Oct 1, 2026. USDA published FY2025 rates on June 24, 2026: 41 states are above 6% and the national rate is 10.62%, and states above 6% must file remediation plans. States are visibly buying: Alabama DHR posted a QC assessment and training RFP, and NC's one-click 'close old deduction' prompt has been used more than 20,000 times, which shows targeted micro-interventions get adopted.
revenue_model: Year-1 state pilot of $60-90k for 12-15 named counties (verify it sits under each state's small-purchase limit). This expands to statewide at $250-400k a year. Counties outside the state contract pay $150-300 per worker, and new-hire certification is $250 per hire. All prices are unvalidated, so get the budget line from the CQI director before writing case #13. Realistic ceiling is about $10-20M ARR across the roughly 40 states above the threshold, so this is the modest-ceiling, fast-to-cash version.
non_obvious_insight: The product is closing the lag, not teaching skill. States already hold the scarcest asset, their own QC findings, and lose months turning it into training. A recall loop (finding, twin drill, completion evidence) cannot be copied by a vendor that only has the generic USDA taxonomy. It is one data-sharing MOU with a state QC unit away, and US Digital Response reports such agreements take 3 weeks to 3 months. Pick the launch state by distance to a cliff times benefit dollars, not by pain: NY at 13% needs a 3-point cut just to reach the 10% tier, while NC at 6.69% can plausibly cross 6%. A 0%-error county is still charged for the state average, so the state CQI unit, not the county, is the customer.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: 20 calls with NC CQI staff, county DSS directors and the state county association, asking who owns a budget line for this and what the last training tool cost. Days 5-15: build 12 drills from public sources only (H.R.1 rule changes, the publicly described stacked-shelter-deduction failure, biweekly wage conversion, household-member removal), and script the 14-day finding-to-drill workflow. Days 15-25: run a 3-county new-hire pre/post pilot with CQI staff as co-facilitators. Days 25-30: hand the state a CAP evidence packet sample and a one-page letter of intent with a price, and ask the CQI director to name the budget line.
lineage: mutation of I1240 ('Flight simulator drills for county SNAP eligibility workers'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Maximus - Accuracy Assistant (SNAP solutions), Code for America - Social Safety Net / SNAP programs, Kognito (sunset) - conversation simulation training, PolicyEngine (open-source US benefit rules engine) and related SNAP repos. White space: Caveat on confidence: my WebSearch budget ran out before I could run any searches, so this is a partial check. It rests on direct fetches of about 15 URLs (the idea's cited sources, Maximus, PCG, PSI, Code for America, Kognito, Relias, Deloitte, Route Fifty) plus GitHub repo searches. Several sites returned 403, 404 or 503. It could not cover Crunchbase, Product Hunt, YC or TechCrunch, or find startup names. The absence of a found direct competitor is therefore weaker than a full search would give, and should be re-checked with searches such as 'SNAP eligibility worker training simulation', 'benefits caseworker AI roleplay startup', and 'eligibility training' RFPs before the founder commits.

What looks unserved: (1) No product I found gives eligibility workers a daily, scored, synthetic-case drill tied to the specific federal QC error elements (wages, household composition, shelter and address changes) with per-worker error-type heatmaps. Maximus's Accuracy Assistant explicitly works 'side-by-side' in live cases and does not train. Code for America and PolicyEngine are systems and rules tools. Kognito-style simulation vendors never targeted eligibility work. (2) Nothing found ties practice performance to documented CQI or corrective-action-plan evidence, which NC's official explicitly asks counties for ('documenting, documenting, documenting'). (3) New-hire ramp-up: Kansas cited turnover and caseworker training complexity as drivers of its errors, and no product measures time-to-competency.

The main threats are structural rather than competitive: (a) the real buyer is the state, which typically owns training (state academies, mandated curricula, training environments in the state eligibility system), and county discretionary budgets may not cover $12k-25k; (b) Maximus or a state's existing LMS vendor could add a practice module; (c) policy variation across states (BBCE, standard utility allowance, county practices) makes per-state case libraries costly to build and keep current; (d) an open-source rules engine (PolicyEngine) lowers the barrier for copycats. | How this version avoids them: Maximus Accuracy Assistant flags risk inside the live workflow and does not train. We use the same error patterns upstream and can pass them to Maximus, so it is a channel or acquirer, not a rival. State academies and NC's monthly QC webinars are free supply, but they are lecture-style with no per-worker measurement. We arm the CQI staff who run them and produce evidence they cannot. Code for America and PolicyEngine are flow and rules tools. PolicyEngine is a commodity input to our scoring, and the moat is the state's own finding library plus the audit trail. Kognito sold soft-skill simulations with no dollar metric. Every drill here is tagged to a QC element and its cost-share exposure. PCG, PSI and Deloitte sell consultant hours, while this is a persistent loop and evidence record priced below a single consultant week.

title: The Pharmacy-Verified Reimbursement Index
one_liner: A furnisher-funded bureau, like a credit bureau for PBM payments, that turns what pharmacies actually pay and are actually paid into a reference index that state laws, Medicaid rate-setting and transparent-PBM contracts can cite, launching with a per-state Underwater Index sold to pharmacy associations for the 2027 legislative sessions.
customer: First six months: state pharmacy associations and their legal and lobbying arms in 3-5 states with active 2027 PBM agendas, at $25-60k per state per year. Next: state Medicaid pharmacy programs and state employee plans rebasing dispensing fees and ingredient-cost basis, departments of insurance enforcing below-cost and pay-parity laws, and TPAs, consultants and transparent PBMs that want an external yardstick. Eventually: contracts that reference the index directly. Contributing pharmacies pay nothing and get a dividend.
problem: Everyone who needs a reference price for pharmacy reimbursement relies on an interested party or a slow survey. NADAC is a voluntary survey of acquisition costs that says nothing about dispensing cost or what any PBM actually paid. State cost-of-dispensing studies are periodic, commissioned from consultants, and stale by publication (typically low-to-mid six figures each; verify). Legislators cannot say how many claims are paid below cost or by whom, so reimbursement-floor and pay-parity laws are enforced only by complaint. PBMs face no neutral definition of a fair payment. The parent's insight (pharmacies hold the ground-truth ledger) is stronger as infrastructure than as a one-off audit.
solution: Pharmacies use the free local-first margin report (same ingestion as a per-pharmacy tool) and opt in to contribute monthly aggregates: paid price and invoice cost per NDC per PBM network per state, plus optionally allocated cost-to-dispense. The bureau publishes: (a) a State Underwater Index (share of claims paid below acquisition cost, by PBM, only where 10+ pharmacies and 5+ per PBM cell contribute, with a 90-day lag); (b) an invoice-based acquisition cost index by NDC-week; (c) a quarterly cost-of-dispensing panel; (d) a regulator API to test whether a network paid below the index in a given month. Design floor for antitrust: a third-party-run exchange following the withdrawn 1996 health-care information-exchange conditions (5+ contributors, no contributor over 25% weight, data 3+ months old), plus counsel sign-off. Credibility: published methodology, an independent standards board (pharmacist, health economist, antitrust counsel, ex-regulator) and a sample audit by an accounting firm. Flywheel: an association buys the evidence pack, a law cites the index, the regulator needs the feed, contracts reference the index, and more pharmacies contribute for the dividend (25% of index revenue, pro rata by verified contribution).
why_now: A wave of state PBM reimbursement and transparency laws has arrived just as closures (Rite Aid gone, Walgreens closing about 1,200 stores, Drug Channels' August 2026 'K-shaped shakeout') give legislators a reason to demand numbers; 2027 sessions open in January and associations need evidence in Q4. The cost stack has collapsed: surveying a few hundred pharmacies by questionnaire costs six figures, but reading remits and invoices they already hold costs cents per claim now that OCR and LLM parsing handle messy formats and local-first processing removes the custody objection. This is a 2026 unlock, not a 2019 one.

State Medicaid and employee-plan data licenses: $100-400k per state per year after a track record. DOI compliance feed: $50-150k. API licenses for TPAs, consultants and transparent PBMs: $25-100k. Index-in-contract licensing: about $0.02-0.05 per member per month, comparable to index-licensing models in other markets. Pharmacies: free plus a 25% revenue dividend. The more PBM-owned pharmacies dominate the market, the more the independents' ledger is the only independent counterfactual.

title: Human Bench Network for AI Agents
one_liner: An API-fronted network of laid-off expert bench scientists who run ad hoc wet-lab experiments for AI agents and return machine-readable execution records.
customer: AI-first biotechs, AI-for-science startups and university groups (5-60 people, seed to Series B) that run agent swarms but have no wet lab; later, programs adjacent to frontier labs.
problem: Agent swarms now propose far more experiments than anyone can run. Anthropic's run went from 200,000+ reverse transcriptases to 20 candidates using ~950 agents in 21 hours. Stanford's Virtual Biotech (37,000 agents, Science, Sept 17, 2026) says the next step is testing findings in real labs. Cloud labs and robots handle fixed assays, but not ad hoc molecular biology: Anthropic itself found robotics less conducive to ad hoc workflows and kept human scientists at the bench. Human review and bench work are the bottleneck.
solution: Ticketed experiments through an API or MCP endpoint. The agent proposes a protocol and a senior scientist does feasibility triage. A vetted contractor then runs it at sublet or surplus benches, BSL-1/2 only. Each job returns a signed record that separates AI proposal, human edit and physical execution (deviations, photos, instrument logs, raw data). Fixed price per experiment. Start with commodity molecular biology: cloning, small-scale expression and purification, ELISA/BLI/qPCR, enzyme activity, bacterial and cell-culture assays.
why_now: Frontier labs and Stanford now say publicly that bench execution is the bottleneck. BioSpace tracks 15,000+ biopharma job cuts across 50+ companies in 2026, which supplies skilled hands. The OpenAI Foundation plans to distribute $1B by year-end through Public Data for Health, which creates grant-funded demand for data generation. Lab Manager notes there is no sign-off standard for AI-directed experiments, and this record format supplies one. Anthropic has said it wants to work with other scientists.
revenue_model: $1.5-8k per experiment at roughly 35-45% gross margin, monthly retainers with minimum volumes for agent-heavy customers, and a premium for 48-hour turnaround. The platform keeps a take rate on contractor labor.
non_obvious_insight: Compute is now nearly free compared with bench throughput, and robots failed as the universal answer because real biology is ad hoc. The defensible assets are a pre-vetted pool of humans and a structured execution record that agents can learn from. Humans become the last-mile actuator for AI. Adaptyv and cloud labs cover single fixed assays; nobody sells the long tail of one-off experiments.
first_30_days: Recruit 10-15 laid-off molecular biologists in Boston, SF and San Diego through layoff trackers and alumni groups. Rent 2-3 sublet benches or surplus CRO benches. Define three ticket types with fixed prices. Pitch 10 AI protein-design and agent startups and close 3-5 pilots. Aim for the first 20 paid experiments and publish the sample record schema.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Adaptyv Bio (Adaptyv Biosystems), Ginkgo Bioworks (Cloud Lab and Datapoints), Emerald Cloud Lab, Science Exchange and Scientist.com (CRO marketplaces). White space: Things I did not find. I could not run WebSearch (the session budget of 200 was used up), so this comes from Google News RSS queries and direct page fetches. I did not check Crunchbase, YC's directory, Product Hunt or GitHub in depth; a GitHub repository search returned nothing.

1. No funded company sells human-executed, ad hoc, arbitrary-protocol wet-lab work through an agent-native ticket API with a fixed price and a signed record separating AI proposal, human edit and physical execution. The nearest pieces are split across companies. Adaptyv has the agent API but runs standardized automated assays. CRO marketplaces have custom human work but run on quotes and SOWs. Transfyr has the execution-record capture but no labor. Emerald and Ginkgo have flexible automation but were not found to offer human-run ad hoc work to agents.
2. The long tail beyond fixed assays is the actual gap. That means multi-step, protocol-specific molecular biology that a robot cannot be programmed for in time: novel enzyme or nuclease activity validation, cloning plus cell-free expression plus a custom activity readout, and unusual cell-culture assays. Anthropic's post confirms this is where a frontier lab keeps human scientists.
3. Nobody I found sells biosafety-screened human execution of AI-proposed protocols as a service, even though oversight of AI-directed experiments is in the news (Lab Manager, 'Biosafety Oversight for AI-Directed Lab Experiments', Sept 28, 2026; Frontiers paper on automated-lab security tiers).

Risks to the idea's own claims:

Skilled hands are still available, but the 'layoff wave' supply story is weakening (via https://news.google.com/rss/search?q=biotech+layoffs+2026+BioSpace+job+cuts+tracker).

title: Independent Collateral Verifier for Warehouse Lenders
one_liner: Sell the same listing-vs-ledger signal not to the floorplan lender but to the lender's lender: credit funds and banks that fund floorplan and subprime auto lenders and get a borrower-supplied VIN tape they have never been able to check, delivered as a signed monthly verification certificate that borrowers pay for through facility fees.
customer: Portfolio-monitoring and credit officers at credit funds, banks and specialty-finance desks that provide warehouse or revolving lines to independent floorplan companies and subprime or BHPH auto lenders. The chooser is the warehouse lender, and the payer is usually the borrower via a monitoring fee written into the facility, the way custodian and backup-servicer fees already are. The law firms that draft these credit agreements are a second influence channel.
problem: After Tricolor and PrimaLend (Sept 2025), the lender's lender is exposed to collateral that is self-reported by the party with the strongest incentive to overstate it. It receives a VIN-level borrowing-base tape weekly or monthly. It has no auditors and no view into dealers, and field exams are annual, sample-based and weeks stale. It holds the tape but has no line of outside data to check it against. Existing floorplan-side tools are bought by the borrower, so they cannot be independent by construction.
solution: Tape-in, verification-out. The warehouse lender (or borrower on its behalf) forwards the borrowing-base tape it already receives and we return a weekly exceptions report and a signed monthly Borrowing Base Verification Certificate. (1) VIN-level reconcile of every tape VIN against listing history and the borrower's reported paydowns and collections, flagging vanished-from-listing with no paydown. (2) A borrower-level Collateral Integrity Index covering percent of tape VINs vanished-unpaid by age bucket, listing coverage ratio, and trend, benchmarked against the warehouse lender's other borrowers. (3) Because noise averages out at portfolio level, precision required is far lower than for per-VIN dispatch, and low listing coverage is reported as its own finding, not hidden. (4) Escalation: a 'for-cause exam recommended' trigger with a shortlist of dealers for a partner field-exam firm. (5) Contract language kit: a standard 'independent verification agent' covenant and fee schedule for law firms to drop into new facilities and amendments.
why_now: Sept 2025's Tricolor and PrimaLend collapses put verification failure in front of every warehouse lender and investor. Private credit funds now hold large slices of specialty-auto warehouse exposure with small monitoring teams. Facilities are being re-papered and re-underwritten, so a verification covenant can go in now instead of waiting for a renewal cycle. Cheap licensed listing history and LLM tape parsing make a weekly external check a software job instead of an exam-firm engagement.
revenue_model: Monitoring fee of about $3,000 to $6,000 per facility per month ($36k to $72k per year), paid by the borrower through the facility's fee schedule or by the lender directly, plus a $15k to $25k onboarding backtest. Add-ons include a 10 to 15 percent referral fee from partner field-exam firms on for-cause exams, and licensing the anonymized Collateral Integrity Index to ABS investors and surveillance teams. If a niche of 100 to 150 specialty-auto warehouse lenders with 3 to 5 facilities each adopts it, the ceiling is roughly 300 to 600 facilities, or $15M to $30M per year before expanding to retail-auto tapes. These figures are assumptions to test.
non_obvious_insight: The funding-side buyer already owns the one input the product needs (the VIN tape) and has never had a single external data point to check it against. Verification fees are set by the chooser but paid by the borrower, who benefits from an independent stamp that supports better advance rates, so the payer wants it even when the chooser only tolerates it. Once written into facility documents, a fee line like custodian and backup servicer is sticky and renews automatically, which is a switching-cost moat that a per-dealer SaaS tool never gets.
first_30_days: Days 1 to 10, list 40 warehouse lenders and credit funds active in specialty auto from trade press and deal announcements, and line up conversations with two or three finance law partners who draft these facilities. Days 10 to 30, run 10 calls with portfolio monitoring heads and offer a free one-facility 'shadow verification' using a tape they already hold. They email it, and within five business days we return a one-page findings memo covering coverage ratio, vanished-unpaid VIN count and peer benchmark. Also sign a partner field-exam firm for for-cause follow-ups. Success is one lender agreeing to a paid quarter and one law firm agreeing to circulate the covenant language.

title: Neutral Ground Baseline for Foundation Projects
one_liner: A developer-paid, two-sided satellite baseline of every neighboring tower, delivered at the same time to neighbors and insurers, and sold as a line item by the geotech and vibration-monitoring firms already on the job.
customer: Payer: mid-size South Florida condo developers and general contractors (and their deep-foundation subcontractors) on projects with pile-driving, dewatering or deep excavation within about 300 m of occupied towers. Co-buyers: builders-risk and CGL underwriters, MGAs and wholesale brokers who insure those projects. Channel: geotech and vibration-monitoring engineering firms who already write the monitoring plan and can resell.
problem: Neighbor claims are the tail risk of urban high-rise foundation work. Vibration and settlement claims, injunction threats and stop-work fights can add months of construction-loan carry on a $150M-$400M tower. The developer's own crack survey is discounted as self-serving. Underwriters have no independent evidence of pre-existing condition, so they price the whole neighborhood as worst case, or add sublimits, higher deductibles or exclusions for adjacent-property damage. The UM study showed many towers were already sinking at mm/yr for reasons unrelated to any neighbor. Developers cannot prove that, and neither can anyone else.
solution: Neighbor Ledger. At permit or early foundation stage, process the archive for every building in the influence zone (typically 15-40 towers) and issue a neutral baseline package. It goes the same day to (a) the developer and its insurer and (b) each neighboring association through a read-only portal. Neighbors get a free 3-page report on their own tower, which gives them evidence and a reason to stop fighting the permit. Timestamps and data hashes are anchored, so neither side can dispute the record. During construction, a monthly delta report flags any tower whose motion departs from its own trend or from control towers. When a claim is filed, a dispute packet is generated within days. A rule is written into every contract: the company gives identical data to both sides and never testifies for either. Expert work goes to an independent geodesist panel. Priced fixed per project and sold as an add-on line item on the geotech firm's monitoring contract.
why_now: Miami's high-rise foundation boom is running against an unusually alert neighbor base: the 2024 UM study was widely covered, Marenas spent about $20K on sensors after a neighbor started work, and the Estructura June 2026 campaign has associations asking developers for data. Post-Surfside underwriters demand structural documentation, and softening reinsurance capacity makes MGAs hungry for differentiated loss-control tools. Processing cost has collapsed with free OPERA DISP-S1, Sentinel-1 and NISAR data.
revenue_model: $18K baseline per project at permit, plus $2.5K/month during foundation and superstructure phases (about 18 months), so about $60-65K per project against a $150M+ build. Reseller share of 20-25% to the geotech or vibration firm. Insurers and MGAs get a portfolio loss-control dashboard as a $25-50K/year program license, in exchange for a premium credit or a warranty requiring the ledger. Assumed 30-40 new high-rise foundation starts per year across Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach (verify from permit data), so about 12 projects in year one at roughly $700K. Expansion to Tampa, Orlando and Houston follows once insurers accept it.
non_obvious_insight: The parent's flaw was that boards may not want to know. Here the party with the strongest need to know is the developer, whose worst nightmare is a false or mistaken damage claim. A baseline showing the neighbor was already sinking is worth more to the developer than to the neighbor. Neutrality is the product: one record both sides accepted is worth more than two competing reports, the way an escrow agent is worth more than two lawyers. Because every competitor is on one side, refusing to take a side is a position none of them can copy without losing their existing clients. Once about 10 projects and two insurers rely on ledgers, a city or county can make a settlement baseline a permit condition, as some European cities require for deep excavation next to older buildings. That would turn a product into infrastructure (hedge: verify local precedent).
first_30_days: Week 1: list the 6-8 geotech and vibration-monitoring firms with active Miami-Dade or Broward jobs, using their public monitoring plans and permit files. Build unsolicited Neighbor Ledgers for 5 currently active sites from free data. Week 2: pitch each firm 'add this as a line item, you keep 25%, we do all the work.' Meet 4 builders-risk and CGL wholesale brokers and MGAs with a one-page loss-control pitch and one question: would you give a premium credit or require it? Weeks 3-4: close one developer pilot at half price ($9K) on a site in early foundation stage, in exchange for an underwriter introduction, and sign one geotech reseller. Kill test: if no geotech firm will bundle it and no underwriter will credit it, drop the model.
lineage: mutation of I1289 ('Settlement Passports for Florida High-Rise Condos'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Estructura (division of Dorado Services) - TerraIntel InSAR + GeoSIG sensors + GeoSMART, TRE ALTAMIRA (CLS Group; TRE Altamira Inc.), Sixense Satellite / Atlas InSAR (Vinci group), Fugro (InSAR high-rise settlement evaluation and prediction). Sensors installed at start cannot recreate a pre-construction baseline. OPERA is free and coarse and carries no neutral delivery or insurer-accepted format. The moat is insurer acceptance plus the neutrality reputation, and both take time to copy.

title: Neutral Monitoring That Unlocks Backup Diesel Dispatch
one_liner: A permit-to-dispatch package for data center backup generators that bundles neutral fence-line and neighbor-home monitoring with an automatic neighbor payout guarantee, so regulators and neighbors can say yes to more run-hours.
customer: Colo and hyperscale operators in PJM (Northern Virginia, Ohio, Illinois) with 20-500 MW of backup gensets who want to count them as capacity. Secondary buyers are county and state regulators who can make the monitoring a permit condition, and utilities and capacity buyers who need fast MW.
problem: Backup fleets sit idle because air permits cap non-emergency run-hours, and any permit change invites a public fight. Neighbors and regulators distrust operator-supplied modeling. Moratoria are spreading: New York paused permits in July 2026, Texas halted TCEQ data center permits in September 2026, and local pauses exist in at least 14 states. The permit-lawyer playbook alone doesn't win the social license, and neutral monitoring alone doesn't monetize.
solution: Fixed-price 'Dispatch Readiness + Neighbor Guarantee'. (1) Permit headroom audit and modification strategy (run-hour caps, synthetic-minor limits). (2) A 60-day ambient baseline of PM2.5, NO2/NOx and night noise at the fence line and at 5-15 volunteer neighbor homes, with hash-anchored timestamps and a public read-only dashboard reviewed by an outside expert. (3) The monitoring plan written into the permit application as the verification method. (4) A developer-funded escrow that pays households automatically when a verified exceedance coincides with a dispatch or test run. (5) The same telemetry doubles as the third-party measurement and verification for PJM programs.
why_now: PJM cleared 6.8 GW short and wants large loads to bring capacity or be curtailed. Turbines are sold out until 2029-30, so backup gensets are the only large block of capacity that exists today. Simultaneously, permit fights have gone from town boards to governors' offices, and regulators are drafting what evidence counts.
revenue_model: $15k fixed-fee dispatch-readiness audit as the wedge. $40-150k per site for permit and engineering work. $75-150k per site for baseline setup plus $4-10k per month for monitoring. An 8-10% administration fee on the guarantee escrow. 10-20% of the first five years of capacity revenue. At the roughly $325/MW-day cap, a 20 MW fleet is worth about $1.5-2M a year after derating, so the fees are easy to justify.
non_obvious_insight: Emergency-only runtime means expected neighbor payouts are tiny compared with the capacity revenue, so the parametric guarantee is nearly free to fund. Its real job is to turn permission from an adversarial fight into a priced product. The monthly 10-30 minute test runs are a free experiment. Sensors can measure the actual ambient impact of routine test runs before any expansion, giving regulators real measurements instead of dispersion models. The baseline also protects the operator against blame for pollution that came from traffic or other sources.
first_30_days: Pull public Title V and minor-source permits for about 30 colo sites in VA, OH and IL and build the permit headroom map. Retain one air-permitting consultant. Build 10 sensor nodes from off-the-shelf parts (about $1.5-3k each) and co-locate them against a reference monitor. Offer 25 facility and sustainability leads a $15k dispatch-readiness audit that includes a 30-day pilot on one site, and aim to close two. Bring the live dashboard to the first public hearing.
lineage: hybrid of I1172 + I0836 (Neutral Baselines and Neighbor Guarantees for Data Centers + Air-Permit Unlock for Idle Data Center Diesel). Why stronger: The permit playbook alone has long enterprise cycles and depends on regulators trusting the operator. The monitoring business alone competes with KETOS-style sensor vendors and is a cost center for developers. Combined, the monitoring is the missing permission-to-operate evidence, and the permit unlock gives the monitoring a clear ROI, a percentage-of-capacity-revenue upside, and a repeatable per-state playbook that is hard to copy.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: KETOS (SHIELD / KELP data-center water monitoring), Aethair (Aethair PRO, Environet, Thiamis), Envirosuite (ASX:EVS), Kunak. White space: Nobody found sells the bundle, so the status is 'gap' and not 'open'. The sensor and baseline layer is not open: KETOS (about $45M raised) pitches an independent baseline for data centers, Aethair pitches pre-construction baselines, Envirosuite has community dashboards, and consultancies bundle baselines into permitting. The unserved wedge is what sits on top of the sensors. (1) A neutral administrator holding escrowed, tamper-evident data whose governance the county and community accept, unlike developer-hired consultants and unlike opposition-side groups such as CEDS. (2) The Neighbor Guarantee: an automatic, no-litigation payout to households from a developer-funded escrow when a pre-agreed trigger is hit. No vendor, insurer, county ordinance or developer program found does this. The nearest things are Franklin County, Indiana's draft rule (escrow for 24-hour emergency potable water to impacted neighbors, plus developer-funded monitoring wells), one-off buyouts and lump-sum checks. (3) A 10-year, multi-parameter (wells, noise, PM2.5, voltage) record packaged as a permit-condition template that regulators can adopt. Weak points: the sensor baseline will commoditize; attribution is hard, because well drawdown from drought or other pumping is indistinguishable from data-center drawdown unless the design uses upgradient control wells and pumping records; automatic payouts may look like insurance under state law; and developer counsel may resist a pre-committed payout as an admission of liability. Closest players: Voltus, CPower, Enchanted Rock (ERock), Trinity Consultants (data center and power team). I did about 30 direct page fetches and 2 GitHub searches instead. The GitHub searches found no open-source tool for this. I found no company selling a fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' package for existing data center diesel fleets (permit modification, emissions retrofit financing, telemetry, PJM enrollment and M&V). That is absence of evidence from a constrained search, not proof that none exists.

What appears unserved:
(1) A productized, per-state permit playbook tied to capacity outcomes. Trinity-type consultants sell hourly, per-project permitting. DR aggregators (Voltus, CPower) sell enrollment and revenue share. Generator OEMs and ERock sell hardware. Nobody I found owns the seam between them.
(2) Retrofit financing on the subset of engines that need it.
(3) A permit-headroom dataset across Title V and minor-source files.

The binding constraint is legal, not competitive. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), as summarized from Cornell LII, emergency engines are limited to 100 hours a year for maintenance, testing and emergencies, with at most 50 of those for non-emergency use. The 50 hours cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, and cannot generate income or serve a financial arrangement with another entity. Only narrow exceptions exist, dispatched by local authorities for transmission and distribution limits. Selling emergency-designated diesel as PJM capacity therefore likely requires reclassifying engines as non-emergency, which triggers stricter engine standards (Tier 4 or SCR-type controls), plus state NOx limits and possible major-source permitting. That is why the founder's 'retrofit the subset' step is likely the real cost and risk. It is also why incumbents have stayed away. The wedge exists only where the permit and retrofit math actually closes.

Other risks: PJM DR accreditation rules and limited-duration derating, which I could not verify because the PJM manual fetch returned only a table of contents. Local opposition to diesel. Hyperscalers and utilities choosing gas or battery capacity instead.

title: Subpoena-Ready Rate Cards for Lien-Based Clinics
one_liner: Invert the parent by selling the coder bench to the clinics being attacked, using their own ledgers to defend their prices and build the industry's only record of what LOP care actually collects.
customer: Owner-operators of multi-location chiropractic groups, pain-management practices, ortho groups and physician-owned ASCs in Florida, Texas and Georgia that treat on letters of protection, especially those who have just received a subpoena or whose plaintiff-firm partners ask for 'defensible bills'. Wedge is 3-15 location groups in Houston, Atlanta, Orlando, Tampa and Miami. Plaintiff-firm referral managers act as influencers and channel.
problem: Reform made a clinic's pricing method, LOP arrangements, factoring and referral relationships discoverable. Owners are now deposed on how they priced a CPT code, and 'it is our standard rate' loses against a chart showing 8-15x Medicare. The honest answer is that LOP care is a credit product. The clinic waits 12-24 months, bears loss risk and often writes off 30-60% blindly at settlement. That premium is legitimate but undocumented, and nobody derives it from the clinic's own ledger. Plaintiff lawyers are not billing experts, and today's billing experts are hired after the attack.
solution: Product: LOP rate-card defense. (1) Ledger study: ingest 24-36 months of the clinic's LOP AR ledger from its practice-management export, computing realized collection per billed dollar, time-to-cash and non-recovery by code, attorney and venue. (2) Cost-of-carry model: derive a documented deferred-payment and collection-risk premium from that data. (3) Rate-card rebuild: restructure the fee schedule to a stated formula (local commercial median from payer Transparency-in-Coverage files times the documented premium) with coding hygiene fixes, written up in a dated, contemporaneous methodology memo signed by a certified coder and a health economist or CPA. (4) Deposition-defense packet for the owner and a ready declaration. (5) Annual attestation, quarterly drift check, and a per-bill 'rate-card attestation' clinics can attach. Scope excludes anything that hides referral or funding relationships. Disclosure remains counsel's job, and a healthcare regulatory lawyer reviews the offer for anti-kickback and fee-splitting risk.
why_now: Florida cases post-2023 and Georgia cases post-2025 are producing the first wave of provider subpoenas and depositions about rate-setting and referral relationships. Messy practice-management exports can now be normalized cheaply with LLMs, and payer Transparency-in-Coverage files make a local commercial median computable for free. Neither existed at usable cost in 2019.
revenue_model: Ledger X-ray free. Rate-card study $6.5k one-time. Monitoring and attestation $750-1,500/month per practice. Deposition prep $250/hr. Illustration: 100 clinics at $6.5k plus $900/month is about $1.7M in year one. The 10x layer is data and standard. After 150+ clinics and 30 months of ledgers, publish a quarterly 'LOP Realized Value Index' (free summary, paid detail) sold to carriers, funders, reinsurers and legislators, plus a registry that carriers pay to query. Carriers that agree to a fast lane for attested bills within the index band create a private fee schedule for the schedule-less LOP world, the way workers' comp fee schedules replaced price fights. Balance-sheet optionality later is a fund that buys attested receivables at index-based prices.
non_obvious_insight: The best defense of an LOP bill is explaining why it is what it is, not proving it is cheap, and the party holding the most valuable data on real LOP value is the clinic, not the carrier or the lawyer. Selling to the attacked party is the cheapest way to acquire that data, since a subpoena is a fear purchase with budget behind it. Providers will hand ledgers to a neutral appraiser but never to a carrier vendor, which is counter-positioning that Enlyte and CLARA cannot copy without alienating carriers. The credibility risk is issuer-pays conflict, mitigated by algorithmic pass/fail thresholds, a published methodology, a visible fail rate, a carrier-side advisory seat and a firewall from any case-specific testimony.
first_30_days: Pick Houston and Orlando/Tampa. Build a list of 60 lien-based groups from provider directories and plaintiff-firm referral networks, and approach through state chiropractic and pain-medicine associations and referral managers at plaintiff firms. Offer the free 'ledger X-ray': send an AR export and in 5 days get a one-page showing billed versus collected, time-to-cash and the five lines an expert would attack first. Sign 5 paid studies at $6.5k within 60 days. In parallel, hold 3 carrier claims-executive calls to test whether an attested schedule would be accepted in pre-suit, and one call with a healthcare regulatory attorney on structure and disclaimers.

The nearest product is Enlyte's Demand Package Review. It is a carrier-side workflow product with nurse and analyst review at 3-4 to 10 days. The fetched summary does not settle whether that applies to LOP treatment, so check the statute text. A large part of the Florida 'report' is therefore a Medicare-multiple calculation from free CMS files, which a claims shop or existing vendor could copy quickly. (b) The hospital price-transparency 'why now' is weaker than the idea claims. CMS says enforcement of the new rules starts April 1, 2026 (https://www.cms.gov/priorities/key-initiatives/hospital-price-transparency). But LOP care is mostly delivered by chiropractors, pain clinics, orthopedic groups and physician-owned ASCs, not hospitals. I inferred that from how LOP cases usually work and did not verify it. The defensible professional-fee benchmarks would come from Medicare multiples, payer transparency-in-coverage files or licensed data, not hospital files. | How this version avoids them: Enlyte and CLARA serve carriers and cannot sell to providers without channel conflict, and providers will not share ledgers with them. FAIR Health measures charges and allowed amounts, while we measure realized LOP collections and carry cost, so the index complements it and rebuts the plaintiff's usual-and-customary anchor. EvenUp is plaintiff-side treatment and demand software with no rate-card defense and is a possible channel partner for its firms' referral networks. Turquoise does payer-contracting analytics, not lien care, and is a data supplier with some entrant risk to watch. The closest direct substitute is per-case billing experts (including plaintiff-side JurisPro-type experts). They are hired after the attack and sell single-case declarations, while this is contemporaneous, subscription-based, data-backed documentation that carries more weight than a declaration created after the fact.

title: Port-Level IP Shield for Indie Brands
one_liner: A subscription that registers small brands' trademarks and copyrights with CBP, feeds officers product-identification guides, and turns port detentions into evidence and settlements against the importers.
customer: Indie consumer brands with $1-30M in revenue that get cloned: fashion, toys, beauty, pet, home goods and Shopify DTC brands. They pay a monthly subscription, plus a share of any enforcement settlements.
problem: Small brands fight knockoffs with Amazon Brand Registry and platform takedowns. Those work after the goods have landed and the listings are live. Most never use the cheapest lever, which is CBP itself. Recording a mark or copyright with CBP e-Recordation costs about $190 per class. CBP can then detain suspected counterfeit or lookalike shipments at the port, and the rights-holder can get photos, samples and importer details that support demand letters and lawsuits. In practice, small brands rarely record. When CBP does ask for authentication, the brand replies late, so the goods are released.
solution: 'Port Shield' handles recordation, builds a product-identification guide (photos, tells, label details, authorized-factory MID list) that officers can use, and monitors for CBP detention and seizure notices. It answers authentication requests within CBP's short response windows, and sets up lever-rule protection against gray-market goods where it applies. It also runs a port exposure scan: lookalike listings on marketplaces matched against public bill-of-lading data to find who is shipping them into LA/Long Beach. When CBP detains a shipment, it packages the importer identity and evidence for partner IP counsel to send demand letters, and takes a share of settlements.
why_now: Generative AI has made cloning product photos and standing up dupe storefronts nearly free, so knockoff volume against small brands is rising. The 2025 de minimis clampdown, and the statutory repeal scheduled for July 2027, push formerly parcel-shipped knockoffs into entries CBP can actually target and hold. Tariff-era entries also carry much richer line-level data, which improves targeting. Long Beach hit a record August of 919,992 TEUs, so port volume is not shrinking.
revenue_model: $750 setup, then $299-$799 a month by number of marks and product lines. Enforcement adds a 20-30% share of settlements, and IP counsel pays referral fees. A later tier sells port-level counterfeit intelligence to marketplaces and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: CBP can only hold what the rights-holder helps it verify. Officers see thousands of lookalikes and act on brands that have recorded marks, supplied identification guides and answered inquiries fast. Big brands have law firms doing this. Sub-$30M brands do not know the port is a free enforcement layer, and most of the relevant customs rules are written for lawyers, not founders.
first_30_days: Pick two crowded niches, such as LA-based apparel and accessories and Shopify beauty or pet. Run free port exposure scans on 30 brands by matching lookalikes to importers in public BOL data. Cold-email the brand owners with the scan attached. Sign 5-10 brands on a paid pilot, record their marks, and produce the first product-identification guides. Line up one IP law firm as the enforcement referral partner.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CBP e-Recordation and free CBP/IPR Center resources (DIY substitute), Corsearch (Brand Protection), Red Points, OpSec Security / Crane Authentication. White space: Confidence caveat: every WebSearch call was refused because the session's 200-search budget was already spent, so this verdict rests on about 35 direct WebFetch pulls plus prior knowledge. I found no funded startup or incumbent selling a done-for-you, small-brand, monitored CBP program (recordation, ID guide, 24-hour authentication desk, detention monitoring, evidence packaging). That is weaker evidence than a clean search sweep, so rerun searches for customs recordation subscription services, and for the CBP offerings of Red Points, Corsearch and IP boutiques, before building. What looks unserved: (1) Enterprise vendors (Corsearch, CSC, OpSec/Crane, MarkMonitor) sell online takedowns to large brands and none of their homepages mention customs; sub-$30M brands are not their customer. (2) Law firms treat recordation as a one-off filing, not a monitored program with an authentication desk; CBP asks for responses within 24 hours (https://www.cbp.gov/trade/priority-issues/ipr/bestpractices), so speed of response is the real product and it is an operations business. (3) Nobody found connects marketplace lookalike listings to bill-of-lading importers for small brands. Skeptical flags, most severe first: (1) Fee-sharing and unauthorized practice of law: a non-lawyer company taking 20-30% of settlements and receiving referral fees from IP counsel likely conflicts with ABA Model Rule 5.4-style bans on splitting fees with non-lawyers in most US states; get a legal opinion before fixing pricing. (2) CBP acts on counterfeit marks and recorded copyrights, not on look-alike dupes or trade-dress copies, so many indie-brand clones (copied design, no logo) are out of reach and the addressable pain is smaller than the pitch implies. (3) Importer identity: before seizure CBP typically does not give the trademark owner the importer name and address; unredacted images or samples come only after the importer gets notice and 7 business days to respond, and full importation details including importer name and address follow seizure within 30 business days (19 CFR 133.21, https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/19/133.21). BOL matching is the workaround, but public BOL data covers mostly ocean cargo, importers can request confidentiality (from memory, unverified), and much knockoff volume moves as parcels or via forwarders and non-resident importers. (4) Recordation needs a USPTO registration (about $350 per class) or a registered copyright, and many $1-30M brands lack full coverage. (5) The lever is $190 per class and the recordation, ID guide and training routes are free on cbp.gov, so the subscription must sell speed, labor and outcomes, not access. (6) Lever-rule (19 CFR 133.23, https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/19/133.23) covers gray-market goods that are physically and materially different; it does not address knockoffs and is a niche add-on.

title: Materials Capture Ratio: Pay-on-Lift for Flat-Rate Shops
one_liner: Measure what share of the parts a residential plumbing or HVAC shop buys actually reaches a customer invoice, coach the leak out tech by tech and job type, and charge 25% of the measured lift over a frozen baseline.
customer: Owner and office manager of residential plumbing and HVAC service-and-replacement shops with 8-25 trucks and $2-8M revenue. They run flat-rate pricing on Housecall Pro, FieldEdge or Jobber (or ServiceTitan without Procurement/AP) plus QuickBooks Online, and techs pull from truck stock restocked on account at Ferguson, Hajoca, Winsupply or a local house. First job types are water heater replacement and condenser/air-handler swaps, where the standard install kit is well defined (expansion tank, flex connectors, T&P valve, discharge pipe, gas flex, line set, disconnect, pad, whip). Reached through PHCC chapters and owner masterminds.
problem: The parent idea has three weak spots. (1) Retroactive found money is mostly uncollectible. A homeowner will not pay a $40 parts add-on six months after a completed job, so an audit that reports history overpromises. Real value is capturing correctly from now on. (2) Contingency on 'newly captured revenue' cannot be attributed, so owners will dispute the fee. (3) Ticket-to-job matching from emailed PDFs is messy because counter tickets carry a typed job name at best, and these shops have no PO-per-job discipline for a 3-way match. Meanwhile the recurring leak is real and habitual. Techs bill labor from the flat-rate book and forget the $6 valve, the wax ring or the whip, and nobody sees it because the two ledgers (supply-house spend and customer invoices) are never divided into each other.
solution: Lead with one owner-legible KPI, the Materials Capture Ratio (MCR): materials billed at cost divided by materials purchased at cost, by month, tech, job type and supplier. It is computed from two exports and needs no invoice-by-invoice matching. Read-only OAuth into QuickBooks Online pulls supply-house bills and restock POs. A CSV or API export from the field-service software supplies the invoice material lines. Day one output is 'of every $100 of parts you buy, you bill $X', per tech. Then learn the shop's own kit per top-10 flat-rate job type by parsing a sample of supply-house lines with an LLM, and each week send the office manager a missing-parts list: closed jobs whose invoice lacks items the kit says were bought, with the pricebook item ready to add, plus which are still rebillable (open T&M, commercial, home-warranty and maintenance-agreement jobs). Add a pre-invoice nudge in the tech's flow later. Supplier-side price drift, unclaimed return credits and repricing files are a free add-on from the same data, not the headline. Contract: freeze a 6-month baseline MCR from the export, then charge 25% of (MCR lift x purchases x the shop's own average materials markup) for 12 months, with the shop's accountant signing the baseline once. It converts to a $199-499 per month subscription that includes the peer MCR benchmark.
why_now: Tariff-driven list-price moves mean flat-rate pricebooks go stale in a quarter, so owners are already asking where margin went. LLMs make it cheap to learn a shop's per-job kit from messy supplier lines. QuickBooks Online and the field-service platforms now expose APIs and exports, so onboarding takes minutes rather than a consulting project. The 2025 copper, steel and aluminum tariff regime, per the parent's research, made materials cost the most volatile line in a service shop's P&L.
revenue_model: Year one is a pay-on-lift fee of 25% of measured incremental materials revenue over the frozen baseline (no lift, no fee), which pairs a low-risk sale with a clean way to dispute-proof attribution. Then a $199-499 per month monitoring and benchmark subscription. Illustration: a $4M shop that lifts capture by 1-2% of revenue recovers $40-80K a year and we earn $10-20K in year one. If the median shop's gap is under 0.5% of revenue, the hypothesis is falsified within 30 days.
non_obvious_insight: The asset is not the found dollars. It is the rate of capture, a ratio you can compute from two exports without matching one ticket to one job, which sidesteps the parsing problem and the retroactive-billing problem together. Pegging the fee to a pre-agreed baseline ratio makes the contingency indisputable, which the parent lacked. Level is not the point, since warranty parts, callbacks and inventory build legitimately lower MCR. What matters is the delta and the spread between techs on the same job type, and that spread turns a vague back-office audit into a coaching scoreboard the owner can act on Monday morning. Pooled over many shops, the per-job-type kit and the MCR distribution become the cornered data asset.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: recruit 8 shops from PHCC chapters and owner masterminds on Housecall Pro, Jobber or FieldEdge with QuickBooks Online. Get read-only QBO access and one invoice-line export each. Days 7-10: compute MCR by tech and by job type in a notebook and deliver a one-page 'you buy $100, bill $X' result within 48 hours of data. Days 10-20: learn the water-heater and condenser-swap kits from supply-house lines, and produce the missing-parts list for the last 60 days as a coaching artifact, not a bill. Day 14-30: ask each shop to sign a 12-month pay-on-lift agreement with the baseline frozen from the export, and start the weekly missing-parts email. Kill test: if the median gap between the top-quartile and bottom-quartile tech MCR is under 3 points, or shops will not accept the baseline, drop or pivot. Web search was unavailable to the parent researcher, so also manually check r/HVAC, r/Plumbing and Crunchbase for small funded entrants before spending on building.
