title: Tool Passport: Molds That Report Themselves
one_liner: An OEM-owned, tamper-evident magnetic cycle counter and registry that makes every mold or die report its own location and shot count, so an unauthorized overrun shows up on the owner's screen and, in time, verified tools can be financed and insured.
customer: Wedge: US OEMs and PE-owned manufacturers ($50M-$500M) that have just moved, or are moving, tools out of China to US, Mexican, Vietnamese or Indian molders and never want a second breakup. Second user: the receiving nearshore molder, who installs the tag to earn 'verified' status with skittish customers. Later payers: tooling lenders, insurers and procurement teams that require a Passport.
problem: Even after reshoring, the OEM's tools sit in someone else's building with no independent record of how many shots they have run, on which press or when. The molder's own counters and MES data are self-reported. Enforcement is all after-the-fact forensics, which is expensive and easy to dispute. Because tools cannot be verified, they are worth nothing as collateral, cannot be insured on custody, and force OEMs into blunt contracts with minimum order quantities and amortization games.
solution: Phase 1 product, 'Tool Heartbeat', is a magnet-mount IP67 tag with an accelerometer that counts mold-open and mold-close cycles from vibration signatures, geofences the tool, detects removal, stores and forwards data over LTE-M, and reports to a per-tool 'passport': QR plate, serial, photo and fingerprint baseline, custody chain, shot ledger versus POs. Silence is contractually a breach. A model 'Tool Passport Addendum' for MSAs, drafted with a China-facing law firm, gives the OEM tag access and audit rights. Phase 2 uses the ledger as the meter for pay-per-shot billing and escrow, so the molder is paid per verified shot and proves innocence. Phase 3 is the registry as a standard: a VIN-and-Carfax for tools that lenders accept for collateral and underwriters use for custody cover. Phase 4 is Passport-backed tooling finance and custody insurance, where the balance-sheet upside sits. Tools still in China get the Census-and-forensics service from the parent, not tags, until SIM roaming and consent barriers are solved.
why_now: Reshoring has created thousands of just-moved tools whose owners are motivated to prevent a repeat. LTE-M and NB-IoT modules with IMUs now cost roughly $25-45 in BOM for a 3-5 year tag. EUROMAP 77 / OPC UA 40077 machine interfaces make molder-side data available to cross-check the independent witness. The tariff-driven wave of moves in 2025-26 (per the parent research) means a stock of new supplier relationships where the tag can be built into the contract from day one.
revenue_model: Hardware $150 per tag (roughly 60% margin at scale), $10 per tool per month for the ledger and alerts, and $1,000 per site onboarding (QR plates, fingerprint baseline, custody paperwork). A 60-tool OEM pays about $22k in year one and $7k a year after. Reaching $1M ARR takes about 140 OEM-sites, so the early business is small. The upside is in the standard: verified-tool finance fees and custody insurance premiums, plus a 'Passport Verified' seal for molders. This is a longer-dated bet, and the near-term money rests on services and hardware.
non_obvious_insight: The parent asks how to prove theft afterward. The inversion is that a tool is the only expensive asset in manufacturing that reports nothing about itself. A cycle count is a signal the tool already produces every 30 seconds through its own vibration, and no one owns it as a customer-side record. Once an independent meter exists, the honest molder benefits as much as the OEM, because it settles quantity disputes, proves clean custody and lets the molder offer pay-per-shot pricing. That aligned incentive is what makes a standard plausible, where a policing tool would not spread.
first_30_days: Weeks 1-3: build 10 prototype tags from an off-the-shelf LTE-M module and IMU (Blues Notecard-class) in a magnetic housing, about $3k. Validate cycle-count accuracy (target within 1%) on 2-3 presses at a friendly Ohio molder who gets free tags and 'Passport-ready' status. Weeks 2-4: pre-sell 3 OEM pilots at $2,400 for 10 tags plus a year of service with a refundable deposit, using the Reshoring Initiative and Ohio plant-manager networks. Draft the Addendum with one law firm. Use the $2,500 Marketplace Overrun Audit as the top-of-funnel cross-sell. Kill signal: vibration counting cannot reach 98% accuracy across press types, or fewer than 2 of 10 OEMs will sign a pilot.
lineage: mutation of I0552 ('Supplier Divorce Protection: Tool Census and Overrun Forensics'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Harris Sliwoski (China Law Blog), Alitheon (FeaturePrint), Red Points, Corsearch (Zeal 2.0, Investigations 360, Distribution Control). I also could not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or open-source repos. The findings below come from about 25 direct page fetches, so treat 'nobody does this' as unproven. The vendors most likely missed are the many small China-based QC and sourcing agents that sell 'mold audits' and 'mold relocation', plus PI and investigation firms (Kroll-type). Alitheon authenticates individual items and has no way to know a tool's shot count or location, so their tech becomes a possible fingerprint tier. QIMA does periodic audits, so it becomes the install and spot-check subcontractor. Sourcify and sourcing agents are a channel, because provable custody helps their nearshore programs.

title: Private Road Agreements That Save Rural Closings
one_liner: A flat-fee e-sign-and-record service that produces the road-maintenance and shared-well agreements lenders demand, then turns each road into a dues-collecting association.
customer: Listing and buyer agents and title/escrow officers in rural and mountain markets (CO, MT, ID, WA, OR, UT, NC/TN mountains, northern New England) pay $400-750 per transaction. Later, the households on each road pay $15-40 a month through the association.
problem: A house on a private road often has no enforceable maintenance agreement, only a handshake among neighbors. FHA, VA, USDA and most conventional underwriters want a recorded, legally enforceable agreement, and similar paper for shared wells, septics and driveways. The appraiser flags the private road and the problem lands on nobody. It surfaces 7-10 days before closing, the neighbors have no reason to cooperate, and the deal slips or dies. Between sales the road decays because nobody can collect dues.
solution: Software plus templated law. (1) Detect private vs public roads from county GIS and identify every benefiting parcel and owner. (2) Use state-specific agreement templates reviewed once by local counsel. (3) Run a multi-party e-sign, remote online notarization and e-recording workflow with a friendly neighbor-outreach script. (4) Add a lender-ready cover letter that answers the standard underwriting condition. (5) Upsell to a formal road association (entity, EIN, bank account, ACH dues billing, reserve tracking, lien rights where state statute allows) and shared well/septic agreements.
why_now: Affordability pushes buyers toward exurban and rural homes, and many of them rely on FHA, VA or USDA financing with strict access rules. Remote online notarization and e-recording are now legal and routine in most states. Counties are refusing to accept new roads into public maintenance. Wildfire-zone insurers and fire districts increasingly care about year-round road access and maintenance.
revenue_model: $495 flat per agreement package, paid by the seller through escrow or by a title partner, plus pass-through recording fees. $250 add-on per shared well, septic or easement agreement. Recurring: $29/month association software plus a payment fee on dues (about 3% + $3 per household per month). Referral fees from title partners.
non_obvious_insight: The road is not the deal-killer. The 4-30 neighbors who each have zero incentive to sign are. So the product is the neighbor-consent workflow, not the document. The other insider fact is that underwriters usually accept a simple recorded agreement signed by a majority of owners with proportional cost shares. You don't need a full HOA. Once a road has bank-account-backed dues, it becomes a sticky recurring customer that nobody else serves.
first_30_days: Pick 2 counties dense with private roads (for example the foothills of Larimer/Boulder CO, or Flathead MT). Pull active listings and cross-match them to county road-class GIS to find listings on private roads. Pay a local real-estate attorney about $2-3k to review one template. Cold-contact those listing agents with a specific message: your listing is on a private road, the lender will ask for this, and we deliver in 7 days. Sign 5 pilots at $495 and 2 title officers as referral partners.

Closest players: PayHOA, Other small-HOA software (Buildium, AppFolio, HOA Start, Vantaca, Cinc and similar), Local real-estate attorneys and title/escrow companies (the incumbent workaround), Generic legal-form sellers (LegalZoom, US Legal Forms, Rocket Lawyer). I used direct page fetches and a GitHub search instead. What I found: (1) No direct competitor turned up in direct fetches, and GitHub has no open-source project for this. (2) The per-deal neighbor-consent workflow (identify benefiting parcels from county GIS, outreach script, multi-party RON/e-sign, e-record, lender cover letter) appears unserved by software. Today it is handled by attorneys and title officers by hand, with generic templates from form sellers. (3) The recurring association layer is NOT white space. PayHOA serves 0-25 unit associations at $49/mo with $2.45 flat ACH, against the idea's $29/mo plus 3% + $3 per household (about $3.45-4.20 on a $15-40 dues payment), so the idea's layer costs more per household than the incumbent. The HUD Handbook 4000.1 text I could read (2019 edition, p.184 and p.566 of the PDF) requires private streets to be protected by a permanent recorded easement, ownership interest, or HOA ownership, says shared driveways do NOT require a joint maintenance agreement, and only has the appraiser ask whether a maintenance agreement exists and comment on road condition. So for FHA the real deal-killer is a missing recorded easement (a title/access cure), not the maintenance agreement. I did not verify VA, USDA or conventional rules or any newer HUD revision. The defensible unserved wedge is a title-partner-distributed neighbor-consent and recording workflow for lenders and loan types that do require the agreement, plus an easement/access cure.

title: Appraisal Workfile Trustee for Retired and Deceased Appraisers
one_liner: A neutral custodian that holds a retiring or deceased appraiser's workfiles for 10 years, proves they were never altered, and answers subpoenas, board letters and lender QC requests so the retiree or widow never has to.
customer: Wedge: sole-proprietor certified residential appraisers aged 62+ who have just gone inactive or announced retirement in 3-4 states (TX, OH, PA, CO), plus heirs and executors of appraisers who die or become incapacitated. These people usually already hold a free LIA or OREP retirement tail, so the money risk is covered and the missing piece is the defense file. Scale payers: E&O administrators and state appraiser associations (loss-control benefit). Requesters (attorneys, lenders, boards) pay production fees where rules allow.
problem: USPAP requires workfiles to be retained and retrievable for at least 5 years (or 2 years after a judicial proceeding ends), and regulators can act later. A retiree's copy sits on an aging laptop, a USB drive or a software subscription that lapses. The free tail pays defense costs but does not preserve or produce the file, and a workfile with no independent proof of when it was finalized is easy to attack as backfilled. When an appraiser dies, board letters and subpoenas land on a widow with no idea what a workfile is. Nobody answers a subpoena on the retiree's behalf: software vendors store files, they do not act as agent.
solution: Product v1, 'Seal and Hold': (1) A 60-minute import from a la mode, ClickFORMS or ACI exports or a drive image. Every file is hashed and stamped with a third-party RFC 3161 timestamp, kept in write-once encrypted storage with an index by date, client and address. (2) A custodian agreement naming the Trustee as records custodian and agent for production, plus a notice letter to the state board. (3) A production desk that handles subpoenas, board requests, lender QC and repurchase requests and E&O carrier requests, notifies the retiree or estate, and bills the requester. (4) An estate trigger: named heirs, a death or incapacity switch and pre-filled paperwork. (5) Retention beyond the minimum, with legal-hold extension. Deliberately excluded: trainees, client transfer, earn-outs, tail brokerage.
why_now: UAD 3.6 becomes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 and is pushing veterans to quit rather than relearn. WorkingRE's 2026 survey says 31% plan to leave within 3 years and 57% are over 60, so a predictable wave of exits is starting. Free LIA and OREP tails have made the money side a solved problem, which leaves the file as the remaining exposure. Immutable cold storage and third-party timestamping are commodity-cheap, so intake per retiree is under an hour of ops time.
revenue_model: $695 one-time for 10-year custody including 3 productions (or $19/month). $995 estate or heir rush plan. Extra productions at $195-450, requester-pays where state rules permit, otherwise billed to the retiree or estate. Group license to E&O administrators and associations at roughly $8-15 per insured per year as loss control (needs validation). Cold storage for about 100 GB costs around $1 per month, so gross margin is 85%+ and the real cost is the production desk and counsel. A two-person team breaks even around 500 custodies a year (assumption).
non_obvious_insight: The free tail pays the lawyer, but a claim is won or lost on whether the appraiser can produce a file that provably existed in that form on that date. A retiree's own drive cannot prove non-alteration, while a neutral custodian with hash chains and third-party timestamps can. So this is closer to a notary or escrow than to storage, which is why software vendors paid by the user cannot credibly sell it and why insurers, estates and boards have reasons to care. Once the custodian is named in the retiree's board and carrier paperwork, moving away means new attestations, which creates switching costs.
first_30_days: Week 1: retain counsel for the custodian agreement and a state-by-state memo on retention, board notification, subpoena handling, and confirmation that we are not acting as an appraiser or AMC and no fee-splitting rule applies. Pull public rosters for TX, OH, PA and CO and flag licenses that went inactive or expired in the last 24 months and active licensees licensed 25+ years. Week 2: call 20 of them and pre-sell at $695 with a refund guarantee, then concierge-deliver the first 5 by hand (import 5 years of workfiles, timestamp, issue a custody certificate). Kill rule: fewer than 6 of 20 pay means pivot to insurer-funded only. Week 3: ask LIA and OREP claims managers, two independent E&O agents and one state appraiser association how workfile requests reach them today and whether they would co-brand or fund it as loss control. Meet 3 estate-planning attorneys. Week 4: run a 'What happens to your files when you retire' session through Appraisal Institute chapters and appraiser forums and target 15 paid custodies.
lineage: mutation of I1039 ('Retirement-in-a-Box for Exiting Appraisers'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: LIA Administrators (Appraisal Institute-endorsed E&O program), OREP (Appraisal Insurance), a la mode TOTAL / Cotality (also ACI, ClickFORMS), Aloft Appraisal. White space: No company found that bundles the four pieces (workfile custody plus subpoena and board-inquiry response, tail, local-knowledge capture, direct-lender client handoff to a supervised successor). Searches for retiring-appraiser succession services, workfile custodian services, and appraiser practice brokers returned only DIY articles from WorkingRE, McKissock, Appraisal Today and NAR.

Specific white space that survives:
(1) Third-party workfile custody and retrieval (agent-of-record for subpoenas and board requests) for retired or deceased appraisers. USPAP requires retention and retrievability for 5+ years, with regulators able to act later, and no dedicated vendor was found. Software vendors and cloud storage only store files, and nobody answers a subpoena for you.
(2) Local, rural or community-lender-funded succession. Aloft, Valligent and Solidifi are national or AMC-centric, not local continuity for a single county.
(3) The retiree-as-mentor stipend and earn-out structure, which none of the trainee programs use.

Specific weaknesses in the idea:
(a) The 'tail is frightening and costly' pain is largely solved for long-tenured appraisers by free LIA and OREP retirement tails. The paid pain is limited to those with short E&O tenure, gaps, or sub-5-year policies. Tail brokerage commissions are therefore thin.
(b) Fee-splitting and finder's-fee rules. Minnesota (82B.20) bans commission-splitting, rebates and finder's fees with appraisers, and other states have similar rules. An earn-out on inherited client revenue and a 20-30% take on trainee fees may be illegal in some states unless structured as a sale of a business or as employment.
(c) Supervisor-of-record is not passive. State rules limit trainee counts (Aloft cites 3 per supervisor), require certification in good standing and the supervisor's own E&O, and make the supervisor take full responsibility. A retiree who stays on as supervisor is not really retired and keeps license, CE and E&O costs.
(d) Client transferability is weak. Appraisal Today notes practices under $200K are 'buying a job', and residential lender relationships are 'fickle'. Most practices sell at 0.33-0.5x revenue with seller financing, and AMC-dependent revenue is not transferable.
(e) Pipeline substitutes are growing: PAREA, AXIS/CRN trainee-inspection reform, Valligent and Aloft paying supervisors. | How this version avoids them: LIA and OREP sell tail money, not file preservation or production, so they are complements and a possible channel rather than rivals. a la mode/Cotality, ACI and ClickFORMS store files for a paying user but do not act as agent of record, sign attestations or answer subpoenas, and a vendor would take on legal exposure for a lapsed customer, so it is unlikely to respond soon. Aloft, Valligent, Solidifi, AXIS and PAREA are all trainee and supervisor plays, and this idea leaves that lane completely, which also removes the supervisor-of-record burden and trainee-count limits. AppraiseItNow buys only non-residential and specialty practices and offers no custody. Reggora and the AMC consolidators (Class Valuation, Atlas VMS) target lenders and AMC capacity, not individual retirees. Dropping earn-outs, percentage-of-trainee-fees and client transfer removes the fee-splitting, minimum-legal and weak-transferability flaws the research flagged.

title: Big-Meter Replacement Fund, Repaid by Verified Uplift
one_liner: A meter-brand-neutral fund buys, installs and owns a utility's worst large meters at zero upfront cost. The utility repays 70% of measured incremental revenue for up to 5 years, with an open verification protocol that makes it an underwritable asset class.
customer: Utilities with 5k-100k connections that know their big meters are old but have no capex or staff. That is most utilities carrying PFAS and lead-line programs. The wedge buyer is a city or district finance director who can sign a no-cost, contingent-payment services contract under their small-purchase limit. Later, infrastructure lenders and the SRF or muni-lease programs that co-finance the fund.
problem: Replacing a large meter is a financing problem, not an information problem. A top-quartile large meter (3-10 inch) costs about $5-25k installed and can recover $6-15k a year in missed water and sewer revenue, which is a payback of about 1-2 years. Yet it stays unfunded. The benefit lands in the revenue line that nobody budgets as upside, while the cost hits scarce capex competing with lead lines and PFAS treatment. Council needs a procurement, an appropriation and a crew. An audit like the sharpened version tells them what to fix, but leaves them to fund and execute it. ESCOs bundle it into large projects with the vendor's own hardware, and meter vendors finance only their own meters.
solution: Underwrite: the screen ranks candidate meters by expected uplift and only meters with payback under about 2 years enter the fund. Verify: an open measurement and verification protocol (pre-swap on-site accuracy test at three flow rates, post-swap test, then 12 months of billing versus matched peer accounts) in the style of IPMVP for energy. Fund: the fund buys meters through distributors at volume and pays independent plumbers and a test subcontractor for the swap. Repay: the utility pays a metering-service fee of 70% of verified incremental revenue per meter, for up to 60 months or until 1.8x of capital is returned, never more, then owns the meter. Payments are contingent, not debt, and recovery is prospective, so no back-billing. Every swap adds a before-and-after label to the yield model, which lowers the cost of capital. Later, pool contracts and sell them to infrastructure debt or bank warehouse lines.
why_now: Revenue-backed, measured-savings financing has already worked for solar PPAs and energy performance contracts once a standard M&V existed. Water meters have none. Utilities are capital-starved by PFAS and lead-line mandates and need off-balance-sheet fixes. AMI interval data makes before-and-after verification cheap enough to sell to lenders. Data engineering means a small team can build the underwriting model, and distributors are eager to move meter volume.
revenue_model: Return on deployed capital: assumed 25-30% net unlevered (about $9k average installed cost, about $6k a year of measured uplift, 70% share, 2-2.5x lifetime multiple, less yield and dispute losses). Fees: 3-5% origination and a verification fee per meter. Later: a warehouse line then securitization of the contract pool. Data licensing of the accuracy-by-model-and-age dataset to lenders, consultants and vendors. Start-up capital: a $250-400k first pilot from angels or a revenue-based lender, plus extended payment terms from a meter distributor.
non_obvious_insight: An accurate large meter is a small, measurable cash-producing asset with almost no credit risk, because its yield, not the city's credit, pays it back. What is missing is a trusted way to measure the yield. Whoever writes and owns the verification protocol and holds the labeled before-and-after data has a standard-setter's position and a compounding cost-of-capital advantage: each verified swap makes the next loan cheaper. Meter distributors are suppliers and floor-plan lenders here, not enemies, because the fund is a volume buyer that creates demand they cannot create.
first_30_days: Write v0.1 of the verification protocol as a 2-page public document and get two reviewers: a water-loss practitioner and a municipal attorney (to review the contingent service-contract form and the state's non-appropriation rules). Get 90-180 day terms from two distributors on 25 large meters and a rate for a test-rig subcontractor. Run free top-100 scans for 6 utilities of 10-40k connections and pick the one with the best yield and a cooperative finance director. Propose a no-cost 25-meter pilot with 70% of verified uplift for 60 months. Line up the first $250-400k. Aim to have the pilot contract on a council agenda inside 90 days.
lineage: mutation of I0388 ('Contingency Hunters for Unbilled Water Revenue'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Itron (Temetra Analysis / Non-Revenue Water portfolio), Badger Meter (BEACON, OneNetwork), Master Meter (Harmony Encore MDM), Metron-Farnier (WaterScope). White space: Important caveat: my WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before any of my searches ran. This verdict rests on about 20 direct page fetches and GitHub repo searches, not on broad web, Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt sweeps. Treat 'no direct competitor found' as unconfirmed, and do a manual pass on Crunchbase, YC and RFP portals before committing. What I did verify: (1) I found no vendor selling a contingency-fee service that joins assessor roll, footprints, imagery and the billing system to produce named unbilled addresses for water utilities. (2) The metering and analytics incumbents (Itron, Badger, Master Meter, Metron) sell software tied to their own hardware, with no evidence of a ranked, dollar-denominated, legal-ready recovery list or contingency pricing. (3) The GitHub search for open-source tools found nothing relevant. Contract meter-testing firms and meter distributors run large-meter testing and right-sizing programs, usually to sell replacement meters. Small local billing-audit shops may exist. Genuinely unserved: an independent, outcome-priced screen of large-account meter accuracy that ranks specific accounts by expected dollars using consumption history, and that does not depend on one meter vendor's hardware. Ghost-parcel discovery is the weaker half. A structure with no account is rare where permits trigger taps, and an ADU on a shared meter is usually already billed on consumption. Back-billing is politically and legally messy, and some jurisdictions restrict contingency contracts. The larger risk is structural (yield, procurement law, optics), not competitive. | How this version avoids them: Itron, Badger, Master Meter and Metron sell meters and analytics, and financing tied to their own hardware would cannibalize their revenue models. They also cannot credibly say the installed base under-registers. Ameresco and other ESCOs bundle AMI and big-scope projects with slow cycles and vendor hardware, and they typically pursue larger projects, so our small verified-uplift tickets sit below their minimums (unverified). Bank lease-purchase programs and SRF loans make the utility carry the yield risk and need appropriation and procurement, whereas ours are contingent payments. EagleView and BlueConduit are data vendors with no capital. Consultancies advise but do not fund. AWWA's free audit is system-level and identifies no accounts. The independent M&V protocol and the private labeled dataset are the moat.

title: Evac Cash: Payout When Ordered to Evacuate
one_liner: A few dollars a month buys a $500-$2,500 wire within hours of an official mandatory evacuation order for your address, covering hurricane, wildfire and burn-scar flood orders.
customer: Renters and lower-to-middle-income homeowners in evacuation zones: Gulf and Florida surge zones, Western wildfire-urban-interface neighborhoods, and LA burn-scar areas. Sold to individuals, through employers of hourly staff (hospitals, hotels, nursing homes, grocers), and through credit unions or municipal 'evac funds'.
problem: Evacuating costs $1,000-$3,000 (gas, hotel, lost shifts, pet boarding) and the money is needed before any claim exists. Cost is a common reason people stay, so the people most exposed are least able to leave. Civil-authority and additional-living-expense cover is slow, receipt-based, often conditional on nearby damage, and many renters lack it.
solution: A parametric contract whose trigger is a legal act. If your geocoded address sits inside a polygon under a mandatory evacuation order, or an NWS flash-flood emergency for a burn scar, the platform pays via FedNow/RTP or a push-to-card within hours. Zone data comes from county emergency-management systems (evacuation-zone platforms and state zone maps). Tiers are priced by zone frequency, with one payout per event per address and a simple app that alerts you and shows your zone. Underwritten via a licensed MGA and fronting carrier, first as employer group policies.
why_now: Address-level, machine-readable evacuation zones are now common. FedNow/RTP make hours-not-weeks payouts cheap. The LA fires of January 2025 made burn-scar exposure vivid, and NOAA CPC/IRI's September 2026 outlooks show a greater than 90% chance of a very strong El Niño this winter, which means heavy rain on fresh burn scars and flash-flood/debris-flow evacuation orders. Parametric reinsurance capacity is plentiful and MGAs want small-ticket distribution.
revenue_model: Premium of roughly $3-$15 per month depending on how often each zone is ordered out (about 1.3-1.5x expected payout), or $1-$3 per employee per month on group plans. The company keeps an MGA commission of 15-25%, plus municipal, nonprofit and employer-funded policies for vulnerable residents. Later it can sell zone-frequency data to emergency managers.
non_obvious_insight: The best parametric trigger is a legal act, not a physical measurement. An evacuation order is binary, public, address-specific and timestamped, so basis risk nearly vanishes. Paying people to leave also changes behavior and saves lives, which makes employers and governments willing co-payers, so the product has two buyers instead of one.
first_30_days: Sign a parametric MGA and fronting carrier. Build the polygon match and instant-payout flow on public evacuation-zone data. Pilot a group policy for about 200 hourly workers at one Gulf hospital or hotel employer and one credit union serving a LA burn-scar community. Offer emergency-management agencies a free 'what zone am I in' tool for distribution. Goal: 500 covered addresses before peak rain season.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Arbol, FEMA Individuals and Households Program (Serious Needs / Displacement Assistance), Homeowners and renters ALE / civil-authority coverage (State Farm, Assurant, Lemonade and other carriers), Jumpstart (parametric earthquake, California). White space: Verification is incomplete, so treat this as a provisional gap verdict, not a confirmed one. I found no product that pays a flat cash amount to an individual within hours because a mandatory evacuation order covers their address. Every adjacent player triggers on something else. Parametric platforms use physical measurements. FEMA and GiveDirectly pay after the event and need an application or a declaration. Homeowners and renters ALE and civil-authority cover is receipt-based. The unserved wedge is the legal-act trigger, paid out as a flat amount before the trip, to renters and hourly workers, funded by someone other than the individual (county or state emergency management, Medicaid and Medicare Advantage plans, landlords or property managers, credit unions, philanthropy). That funder-pays model is the specific space I found nobody in. Main risks: a carrier could add a flat 'evacuation expense' rider to renters policies, and evacuation-zone data is held by vendors and counties, some under licensing terms that were not checked.

title: Agency E&O Insurers Fund AI-Exclusion File Reviews
one_liner: The insurers and endorsed programs that cover insurance agencies pay to put an AI-exclusion review and a client-acknowledgment file behind every commercial renewal their insured agencies handle. It is funded as loss control, in the way cyber insurers fund security scans, and the agency pays little or nothing.
customer: Payer: underwriting and program managers at insurance-agency E&O carriers and MGAs, and the state independent-agent associations that endorse an E&O program to their members. Users: the insured agencies with 5-100 staff. Buyer chain: the party who bears the cost of failure-to-warn claims pays, and the party who does the work receives the tool.
problem: Agency E&O carriers will pay defence costs and settlements when a client discovers, after an AI-caused loss, that the renewal quietly excluded AI and nobody told them. The exclusions are silent (the premium barely changes), they arrive in mass on 1/1/2027 renewals, and the claims will surface in 2027-2029. Even where the duty to advise is weak, defence costs are incurred anyway. Today these carriers have only PDF advisories and webinars, no data on whether any insured agency did anything, and no view of aggregate exposure across their book.
solution: A white-labelled program, called the 'Exclusion File' in the carrier's brand, with three parts. (1) Agency workflow: the agency forwards the renewal quote or policy PDF and receives the diff, the breadth score and a gap letter. The client e-signs an acknowledgment, either accepting the exclusion or asking for affirmative cover or a negotiated carve-back. Everything is stored in an audit-ready vault, which is the classic E&O defence of documented advice. (2) Carrier dashboard: the share of insured agencies enrolled, the share of commercial renewals reviewed, unresolved acknowledgments, and anonymised aggregate exclusion prevalence and breadth by line and by carrier form. It shows the carrier's own exposure. (3) Underwriting hook: a supplemental question on the E&O application, 'Do you review renewals for AI exclusions and retain client acknowledgments?', and an optional rate credit or deductible break for agencies that complete the program on 90% or more of their commercial renewals. The diff engine underneath is the same as in the sharpened offspring, so the marginal build cost is the vault, the e-sign flow and the dashboard.
why_now: The first large exclusion cycle is 1 Jan 2027, so an E&O carrier that acts in Q4 2026 has a defensible risk-control story before any claims exist. Trade and association content already urges agencies to review renewals (Big I on the Verisk rollout, Agents United, IA Magazine on 9 Sep 2026), so the carriers' insureds are being asked to act with no help. Cyber insurers that fund scans and security tooling for insureds have made the loss-control-for-premium-credit model familiar to underwriters. Agency E&O is a concentrated market with few carriers and programs, so a small number of decisions covers a lot of insured agencies.
revenue_model: The carrier or program pays $600-1,500 per enrolled agency per year, plus $25-60k per year for a quarterly AI-exclusion exposure report for its underwriters and reinsurers. The agency pays a $49-99 copay per diff, or nothing where the carrier sponsors it fully. An association that endorses the program takes an endorsed-vendor fee of 10-15% of agency revenue, which is how associations already monetise vendor programs. As an illustration: a carrier insuring 1,500 agencies, 20% enrolled at $900 each, is about $270k a year, plus the data subscription. These figures are estimates to be tested in pilot.
non_obvious_insight: The E&O insurer is the only party in the chain that pays whether or not a court finds a duty to advise, so it does not care about the legal debate that weakens the broker-side pitch. The distribution lever is also the E&O application. Once the supplemental question is on the form, agencies need a compliant answer every year, and this program becomes the standard way to give one. The same carrier-funded logic scales to the next silent-exclusion wave, whether PFAS, cyber war, biometric or another, so the customer can renew and expand on the same integration.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: write a 2-page memo for underwriters with three concrete failure-to-warn fact patterns on 1/1/2027 renewals and a list of the largest agency E&O carriers, MGAs and association-endorsed programs. Book calls through LinkedIn and state association staff, and aim for 5 calls. Days 10-25: offer 3 state associations a free 45-minute webinar, 'AI exclusions on your Jan 1 renewals', which is a cheap way to capture 100+ agencies. Sign 10-25 of them as a pilot cohort using the concierge diff. Days 20-30: take the pilot cohort's hit-rate numbers (how many renewals had a new AI exclusion the agency had not flagged) back to the carriers and associations as a pilot pitch. Ask for a 3-month pilot at about $15k for 25 agencies, or an association endorsement. Carrier cycles run 3-6 months, so the association route generates the first revenue.
lineage: mutation of I1133 ('Renewal Radar for Silent AI Exclusions'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Patra (AI Policy Checking), Quandri, Zywave Apex / Advisor Agent, Testudo. White space: A real gap remains, but it is much narrower than the pitch. Nobody found sells a commercial-lines, broker-facing workflow that (1) takes a book's actual renewal forms schedules, quotes and binders (not just carrier-level filings), (2) detects and normalises AI exclusion breadth for each client, including bespoke wording such as Berkley PC 51380 and unnamed 'AI' language, (3) ties it to a 90-day renewal calendar, and (4) hands the producer a client-ready gap letter and a matched affirmative placement. Pieces exist separately. Patra reads commercial policies for hidden exclusions but is not AI-specific. Quandri and Zywave own the 90-day renewal trigger but show no exclusion-level AI flagging. Testudo and Armilla offer AI-use mapping and placement but only for their own paper.

Three parts of the plan are weak. (a) The SERFF scraper and exclusion database are not a moat. Trades Coverage already compiled 4,078 records for free. Gridex, Certian, Vorp Labs and ShadowLock publish free trackers, and Certian even ships CC BY 4.0 CSV and JSON. (b) A filing shows a carrier adopted a form in a state. It does not show the form is attached to client X's policy, so the real signal is the policy document, not the filing. (c) SERFF filing access covers admitted markets only. Surplus lines is where most E&O, D&O and tech-E&O AI exclusions sit, and it is largely invisible to SERFF.

Wedge that looks unserved: commercial professional-liability and tech-E&O accounts (design firms, law, accounting, software, agencies) where exclusions are broadest and most bespoke, for independent agencies without an in-house risk-advisory team, priced as a renewal-review add-on rather than a filings database. | How this version avoids them: Zywave, Quandri, Patra, Rosella and FurtherAI all sell productivity software or outsourcing to agencies, and none produces carrier-visible compliance evidence, an acknowledgment vault or a book-level exposure dashboard. Testudo, Armilla, AIUC, Mount and Munich Re/Mosaic sell AI liability cover and court brokers to sell it, which makes them conflicted advisers for an E&O insurer. This is neutral and earns no placement commission. The free trackers (Gridex, Certian, Vorp Labs, ShadowLock, Trades Coverage) are content marketing and do not produce a per-client acknowledgment record. Their data is a free input here. The real competitor is the carrier's current PDF advisory and webinar, which is non-consumption of any real workflow. SERFF vendors (InsuranceFiling, Filing360, FilingRamp) sell to compliance teams, and I found nobody selling to agency-E&O underwriters.

title: Consent Ledger for Land-Scheme Family Cohorts
one_liner: A cohort-priced heir-consent ledger sold to the family 'treasurer' of heirs from ONE 1960s-80s land-buying company or settlement scheme, with a partner law firm as the legal entity of record and a recurring Title Watch on top.
customer: The 'family treasurer': the salaried eldest or most solvent sibling (30-55, in Nairobi, Nakuru, Dallas or Dubai) of a family whose parent or grandparent was an allottee or member of one named land-buying company or settlement scheme in one county (pick one scheme in Murang'a, Kiambu, Nakuru or Trans Nzoia through the founder's own church/alumni/clan network). Distribution partners are the scheme's officials and welfare committee. One partner law firm is the entity of record for all legal work.
problem: Judges flagged three flaws in the parent: thin unit economics (field trips per single estate eat the KES 15-25k fee), the Advocates Act risk of a non-lawyer company selling a 'court-ready bundle' (from memory, unverified), and unproven diaspora willingness to pay. The underlying pain is real but narrower than 'succession': the blocker is proving that all 8-20 heirs were found, asked and agreed, and getting them to sign at all. There is also a sharper trigger than paperwork guilt: land in a dead man's name is an easy target for forged transfers and brokers, and absent children fear waking up to find it sold. A generic 'succession kit' has neither the density to be profitable nor a legal shape that survives scrutiny.
solution: Three steps, each cheap to buy. (0) 'Title Check', KES 1,500 over WhatsApp: photo of the title or parcel number, official search (about KES 500 fee, verify), LLM read of the result, one-page plain-language answer: registered owner, is that person dead, who must be involved. (1) 'Consent Ledger', KES 18k (KES 14k cohort price when 8+ estates from the same chief's location are booked): Kenyan name-variant-reconciled heir map, list of required consents, and a live status board the treasurer shares in the family WhatsApp group ('9 of 14 heirs signed, 3 outstanding, reasons'). A home-area agent runs one scheduled 'signing day' per chief's location per month for chief's-letter requests, ID copies, thumbprints and video consent; heirs elsewhere sign by ID-video on WhatsApp witnessed by the nearest agent. Output is a non-legal 'Consent and Kinship Evidence Pack' with a dispute flag (silent heir, second household, contested claim). The partner law firm receives the pack through a case-management seat, drafts, files and shepherds the case, and bills its own scale fee directly; the company never drafts affidavits or quotes legal fees. (2) 'Title Watch', KES 4k per parcel per year: alerts on registry changes plus a caution/restriction workflow run through the advocate. Asset discovery (SACCO, coop, UFAA letters) is a flat add-on sold only after grant, since UFAA beneficiary claims need the confirmed grant first.
why_now: LLMs now read scanned titles, IDs and share certificates and reconcile Kenyan name variants for cents a page, and drafting copilots (Wakili-Intel appeared July 2026 as a hobby project) are commoditising the paperwork, so the scarce, defensible piece moves to field evidence and multi-heir consent, which is still custom work. The settlement-scheme allottee generation is dying now. WhatsApp Business plus M-Pesa/card make small cross-border payments routine, and digitised searches (Ardhisasa; coverage to be verified) cut registry running. None of this worked in 2019: reading messy scans and chatting in Swahili and English at this cost did not exist.
revenue_model: Ladder per estate: KES 1.5k Title Check, then KES 18k ledger (14k at cohort density), then KES 3k flat advocate seat fee per file (software and case management charge, explicitly not a fee split; verify with counsel), then KES 4k/yr Title Watch, then KES 5k asset-discovery add-on after grant. Assumption to test: at cohort density, field plus search plus ops cost is about KES 7-8k per ledger versus KES 12-15k for one-off estates, giving roughly 45-55% gross margin and about KES 26-30k first-year revenue per estate. A county team (coordinator, 2 agents, share of ops, about KES 3M a year) breaks even near 200 estates a year, which one large scheme can supply. Title Watch gives recurring revenue that the parent lacked.
non_obvious_insight: The unit of production is not the estate but the chief's location. Neighbouring estates in one scheme share the same registry, chief, original allottee list, surnames and often the same feuds, so every ledger makes the next one cheaper and better (name-variant dictionary, known-disputer flags, chief relationships). That density economy is invisible to per-estate advocates and to national software. Second, the treasurer is buying a status board, not paperwork: it turns family guilt and pressure into visible progress that nudges holdout siblings. Third, fear of land-grabbing is the purchase trigger, so sell 'protect it' first and 'sort the succession' second.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: pick one scheme and one county through your own family, church or alumni network; sign one partner law firm as entity of record on a one-page engagement letter (advocate bills the client directly; company charges a flat seat fee). Days 7-20: launch the WhatsApp 'Is your family land still in a dead man's name?' Title Check at KES 1,500 in the scheme's clan and welfare WhatsApp groups and in diaspora groups for that county; run 40 checks. Days 20-30: convert to 10 pre-sold Consent Ledgers at pilot price, of which at least 8 in one chief's location; schedule the first group signing day. Core metrics: days from intake to all heirs signed, percent of heirs signed on the first visit, and check-to-ledger conversion. Kill test: fewer than 3 of 40 checkers buy a ledger.
lineage: mutation of I0474 ('Dead Capital: Succession Kits for Diaspora Families'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Luru (open-source 'Kenya's Digital Succession Copilot'), Wakili-Intel (AI drafting copilot for Kenyan advocates), Unclaimed Financial Assets Authority (UFAA), Ardhisasa (Ministry of Lands digital land registry). White space: Provisional, because the web search budget hit its 200-call cap before any search returned results. My evidence comes only from direct page fetches and GitHub repo searches. I found no funded startup, product or open-source project that combines (a) diaspora-paid flat-fee intake, (b) heir mapping across Kenyan name variants, (c) field-agent collection of chief's letters and thumbprint or video consent from 8-20 relatives, and (d) hand-off to partner advocates. The software pieces (family tree, readiness score, drafting copilots) exist only as zero-star hobby repos. Government platforms (Ardhisasa, court e-filing, UFAA) cover filing and claiming but not multi-heir coordination. UFAA's beneficiary claim rule makes succession a prerequisite for claiming a dead person's unclaimed assets, so a succession-first product that unlocks those assets has a logical hook. The unserved wedge is the coordination and evidence-gathering layer sold to the paying sibling abroad. It is still unproven whether ordinary advocates or land-buying-company agents already do this informally, because I could not search for them. | How this version avoids them: Fixed-fee advocates (the only direct competitor) become the channel: they receive consent-complete, dispute-triaged files at zero acquisition cost and keep all legal fees, while the company sells only the field and evidence layer they cannot profitably do at scale fees (chasing 14 heirs across three counties). Luru and Wakili-Intel are zero-star software with no field agents, consent capture or advocates, and drafting is exactly what we do not sell. UFAA is used only after grant as a flat add-on, not a lead product. Ardhisasa and court e-filing are systems we file into, not substitutes; even if Ardhisasa adds guided transmission it will not collect thumbprints from scattered heirs. Defensibility comes from cohort density and the per-scheme kinship dictionary (cornered resource) plus counter-positioning against advocates who cannot make per-heir chasing pay.

title: Unit Tests for Benefit Law: Eligibility System Conformance
one_liner: Invert the drill: aim the same synthetic households and adjudicated answer keys at the eligibility software itself, selling H.R.1 conformance test packs to states and system vendors, with an aim to become the standard test suite that state RFPs cite.
customer: State SNAP and Medicaid policy directors and eligibility-system program managers (the people running user-acceptance testing), then the system integrators that build the systems and the AI-tool vendors selling into agencies. First buyers: 2-3 states whose H.R.1 system releases are due between Oct 2026 and Jan 2027 and that already have a UAT process.
problem: The most expensive error is one the system makes identically thousands of times, which no worker training can fix. NC's eligibility system stacked shelter deductions when caseworkers updated rent, and a one-click prompt fixed it and has since been used more than 20,000 times. H.R.1 forces reprogramming everywhere at once (SNAP work-requirement, noncitizen and utility-allowance rules, Medicaid work requirements and six-month renewals due around Jan 2027) under a 75% state admin share and a 6% error cliff. Vendors test their own work. States rarely have independent, boundary-case test data with signed-off expected outcomes.
solution: H.R.1 Conformance Pack v1: about 250 synthetic households aimed at the edges of each changed rule (income at the threshold, mixed-status households, month-boundary changes, shelter and utility interactions), each with an expected outcome and a citation trail to statute, USDA guidance and the state manual. The state's own policy staff sign off the answer key, so we test state policy against state system and do not have to settle federal ambiguity. Where state policy and federal guidance conflict, we flag it as a second deliverable, a QC-risk memo. Delivery fits existing UAT: scenario scripts and machine-readable fixtures with expected results, plus a divergence report. Later: a regression subscription refreshed on every guidance change, vendor pre-certification, and household-level evaluation sets for AI intake and caseworker-assist tools.
why_now: Every state must change its SNAP and Medicaid eligibility logic within months of each other, and Medicaid work requirements and six-month renewals land around Jan 2027. AI tools are entering benefits workflows and agencies have no household-level ground truth to test them against. USDA's FY2025 numbers (41 states above 6%, 10.62% nationally) make a systemic logic bug politically and financially radioactive. Open-source rules engines (PolicyEngine) and LLM-assisted drafting cut the cost of building cases, so adjudication, not authoring, is now the scarce step.
revenue_model: Per-state pack at $40-120k per major rule change, and a regression subscription at $100-250k a year per program per state. Vendor certification runs at $15-50k and AI-tool evaluation runs at $10-30k. Bottom-up: 50 states x 3 programs x about $300k, so $30-60M ARR is a plausible ceiling, and more if state RFPs cite the suite as an acceptance criterion. Much of the spend can draw federal IT matching funds in system-change budgets (verify per program). Prices are unvalidated assumptions.
non_obvious_insight: Independence is the product, in the way UL or a ratings agency is. Vendors cannot credibly grade their own homework, and states cannot staff independent test authorship, so the cornered resource is the adjudicated, state-signed answer key: expert time that compounds across states and rule changes. Testing the machine reaches a bigger error source than training people, and the same answer-key corpus later powers worker drills, QC calibration and AI evaluation. A standard is reachable because states already buy test scripts and would rather cite a neutral suite than write their own.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: pick 12 H.R.1 SNAP provisions from USDA implementation memos and write 60 boundary-case households. Run them through PolicyEngine and through 2-3 states' public online benefit screeners, which needs no system access. Days 10-18: send each state policy director a private divergence report with 3-5 mismatches and an offer of the full pack. Days 15-30: sign 1-2 paid $25-40k UAT-pack pilots with a state policy or IT lead, and start talks with a system integrator's state account team about pre-certification. Recruit 2 ex-state policy and ex-FNS adjudicators to sign keys.

Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Maximus - Accuracy Assistant (SNAP solutions), Code for America - Social Safety Net / SNAP programs, Kognito (sunset) - conversation simulation training, PolicyEngine (open-source US benefit rules engine) and related SNAP repos. Several sites returned 403, 404 or 503. It could not cover Crunchbase, Product Hunt, YC or TechCrunch, or find startup names. The absence of a found direct competitor is therefore weaker than a full search would give, and should be re-checked with searches such as 'SNAP eligibility worker training simulation', 'benefits caseworker AI roleplay startup', and 'eligibility training' RFPs before the founder commits.

What looks unserved: (1) No product I found gives eligibility workers a daily, scored, synthetic-case drill tied to the specific federal QC error elements (wages, household composition, shelter and address changes) with per-worker error-type heatmaps. Maximus's Accuracy Assistant explicitly works 'side-by-side' in live cases and does not train. Code for America and PolicyEngine are systems and rules tools. Kognito-style simulation vendors never targeted eligibility work. (2) Nothing found ties practice performance to documented CQI or corrective-action-plan evidence, which NC's official explicitly asks counties for ('documenting, documenting, documenting'). (3) New-hire ramp-up: Kansas cited turnover and caseworker training complexity as drivers of its errors, and no product measures time-to-competency.

The main threats are structural rather than competitive: (a) the real buyer is the state, which typically owns training (state academies, mandated curricula, training environments in the state eligibility system), and county discretionary budgets may not cover $12k-25k; (b) Maximus or a state's existing LMS vendor could add a practice module; (c) policy variation across states (BBCE, standard utility allowance, county practices) makes per-state case libraries costly to build and keep current; (d) an open-source rules engine (PolicyEngine) lowers the barrier for copycats. | How this version avoids them: Maximus Accuracy Assistant scores live cases for risk and does not test system logic. Code for America and Nava help states build and communicate rules, not produce independent conformance suites. PolicyEngine is the natural supplier and partner (open-source engine, nonprofit, no state-signed answer keys or sales motion), and its SNAP screener validation is not a state-system acceptance test. Vals AI's Public Benefits Bench (with Code for America and the Center for Civic Futures) is a proprietary question-answering benchmark for beneficiary inquiries. It does not test household eligibility or benefit calculations, so we supply the household-level layer and could partner. System vendors and IV&V firms test their own or generic project deliverables, and independence is our counter-position. The Kognito failure is irrelevant here because the buyer is a funded IT/UAT process, not a training budget. State academies are not substitutes.

title: Notarized Mitigation Records: The Evidence Standard for Wildfire Credits
one_liner: A score-agnostic verification layer where contractors capture signed photos that are cross-checked against imagery and issued as portable machine-readable Verified Mitigation Records, which carriers and certifiers accept.
customer: First, Front Range defensible-space crews, roofers, ember-vent installers and drone inspectors, who pay per job. Then wildfire certification programs (Wildfire Partners, IBHS-style programs) that pay per avoided inspection. Then carriers' appeal desks and underwriters, who read the record through a free API and later pay for ingestion. HOAs and fire-safe councils are the bulk channel.
problem: Homeowners spend $5k-$30k hardening a house and cannot prove it in a way an insurer will accept. Photos and photo-log templates are easy to fake, and AI image generation makes unverified photos worth less each year. HB25-1182 obliges insurers to credit documented mitigation but sets no evidence standard, and on-site inspection capacity is the bottleneck. Contractors cannot promise an insurance credit, so hardening jobs stay unsold.
solution: A web app (PWA first) for contractors and homeowners with guided capture: a checklist of shots for Zone 0/1/2, vents, roof and gutters, taken with signed capture (C2PA-style content credentials, device attestation, GPS, time and heading). The system cross-checks each claim against archived and new imagery and lidar, for example that vegetation was cleared between two dated images or that a roof is Class A. It issues a Verified Mitigation Record as an open-schema JSON file plus a PDF, versioned and portable across carriers. The schema is published under an open licence and co-developed with a fire-safe council. Carrier and certifier readers are free, and acceptance outcomes feed a per-carrier acceptance dataset. The capture layer would use an existing signed-capture SDK, not a new one.
why_now: Generative image tools have made unverified photo evidence untrustworthy. Signed-capture standards and SDKs are now commodity. HB25-1182 turned documented mitigation into a legal object with no format. High-resolution archives and public lidar are cheap enough to act as the independent witness. This is also the inversion of the parent idea: instead of proving a model wrong about the house, prove the house right and let any score-maker read it.
revenue_model: $49-$89 per notarized job, paid by the contractor and passed through in the quote. $40-$120 per avoided on-site reinspection from certification programs. $15-$60 per accepted record from carriers via subscription or API. Agents from a rebuttal desk buy per file. At 300 contractors doing 40 records a year at $65, that is about $0.8M, and the carrier and certifier layers scale it much further.
non_obvious_insight: The reason insurers can decline third-party imagery is that they cannot trust or parse it, not that they are hostile. Give them evidence with provenance, in a schema they can auto-ingest, and the cost of handling an appeal falls. The parent's moat, the concession database, then extends into a network: contractors, homeowners and carriers all gain from a shared format, as with ACORD forms or the Uniform Appraisal Dataset. Because the layer describes the house and not the score, it holds up when Zesty, Cotality or Verisk change their models, and it is neutral in a way a scorer can never be.
first_30_days: Sign 5 Boulder and Jefferson County defensible-space and roofing contractors on a free pilot. Ship the guided-capture PWA with the imagery cross-check. Notarize 60 real jobs. Ask 3 agencies to submit those records in real credit requests and log carrier responses. Propose a 10-file remote pre-verification pilot to Wildfire Partners. Publish schema v0.1 on GitHub.
lineage: mutation of I1148 ('Parcel-Level Rebuttals to Wildfire Insurance Scores'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: FireRisk.ai (RiskIntel AI), DefensibleHome Wildfire Insurance Survival Kit, Defensible Space Score (AACI Group / Five Bays Insurance Agency), Road Home Exteriors 'insurance-grade verification packets'. White space: Nobody found sells imagery-based, parcel-level, insurer-format rebuttal evidence, and nobody sells an agent or HOA 'scan the whole book for likely score errors' workflow. What exists is (a) free or $99 homeowner letter and template kits with no imagery (FireRisk.ai, DefensibleHome, Defensible Space Score), (b) slow on-site certifications (IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home, Wildfire Partners), (c) contractor evidence packets sold with hardening jobs (Road Home Exteriors), and (d) carrier-side imagery scoring (Zesty, Nearmap/Betterview, Cape, Cotality, Verisk) with at most a compliance 'framework' for appeals. Specific unserved wedge: multi-date 15-50 cm imagery that shows a lot's actual condition (irrigated, gravel-scaped, recently cleared) against a 30 m coarse-layer score, formatted for Colorado's 10-day acknowledgement and 30-day decision clock, delivered to independent agents who carry many clients. Genuine caveats that shrink the gap: (1) The premise for California looks broken. AB 75's status page shows it 'held under submission' in Appropriations on 08/29/2025 and no source found shows it enacted (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB75). The CA DOI's own report reportedly says there is no formal appeal process. So the 'statutory appeal right' in CA is unverified and Colorado is the only confirmed regime. (2) Colorado HB25-1182 (signed 28 May 2025, effective 1 July 2026, https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb25-1182) requires disclosure of the score, range and a plain-language explanation of features. It does not clearly require raw model inputs (fuel class, vegetation density), and it does not require insurers to accept third-party imagery. The 'pull the disclosed model inputs' step may be thin, and DOI enforcement is only that the Commissioner may request a copy of a denied appeal. (3) Insurers can satisfy the law with a manual mitigation discount, so a score correction may not change the premium. (4) Free and $99 substitutes cap willingness to pay for $149-299 per file. (5) Zesty, Nearmap and Cotality hold the same imagery and the carrier relationships, so the durable moat is the concession database, not the imagery. | How this version avoids them: Road Home Exteriors and other contractors packaging evidence are customers and distribution, not rivals; this gives their packets carrier-grade credibility. IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home and Wildfire Partners are channel partners, because remote pre-verification cuts their on-site cost. FireRisk.ai, DefensibleHome and the Defensible Space Score offer letters and unverifiable photo-log templates, which the record replaces. Zesty, Nearmap, Cape, Cotality and Verisk are scorers that would consume the record and cannot be the neutral notary because they are the party being rebutted. The real risks are a signed-capture vendor such as Truepic moving into wildfire, and a scorer building its own format. The defences are the wildfire-specific schema, the per-carrier acceptance data, and being paid by contractors for jobs.

title: Solos Refer, We File: National Delay-Suit Bench
one_liner: Invert the tool model: a lawyer-owned litigation bench that takes stuck cases referred by immigration solos, files at industrial speed for about 60% of the boutique price, and pays the referring lawyer a fee share, building a national referral network and the full-cycle dataset as a by-product.
customer: Payer: stuck applicants (post-interview N-400, I-751, I-765, long-idle I-130/I-140) referred by their own immigration lawyer, paying a $2,995 flat fee plus about $455 in costs. Channel: 1-10 attorney immigration firms in NY, NJ and CT that hold stuck clients but will not be counsel of record on a federal suit. Expansion: solos in any state, then boutique firms as overflow customers.
problem: The parent's model needs solos to pay $400 to do something they fear, and the research found no evidence that solos pay for tooling. What solos do have is client trust and a pile of stuck files. Their current choices are to do nothing or to refer the client to a boutique for no reward and the risk of losing the client. Meanwhile the one visible provider (Mandamus.com) is a small boutique with about 30 litigated petitions in 15 years, prices at $5,000 plus $500, and runs no co-counsel program for other lawyers. That leaves a large pool of unserved clients who cannot pay $5,000.
solution: A lawyer-owned litigation bench with the software company as management-services provider under a flat per-case fee (not a percentage of legal fees). The referral flow: a solo submits a stuck case through a 4-minute referral link or a case-management export; the ledger triages it (declining nationality-hold suits and Fifth Circuit I-485 claims); the client e-signs a fee-division consent that names each lawyer's share and the joint responsibility; the bench files within 72 hours, runs the 60-day clock, negotiates consent-order-first, and files the EAJA petition when a consent order supports it. The referring lawyer stays counsel on the underlying application, receives status in their own system, and earns 30% ($900) of the fee. The flat fee covers all litigation including an MTD opposition, matching the boutique's promise. Key legal gate: joint-responsibility fee division rules vary by state (NY 1.5(g) and ABA Model Rule 1.5(e) style), so launch only where ethics counsel clears it.
why_now: AI drafting and docket automation cut attorney time per routine filing from 6-10 hours to about 3 with paralegal support, which lets price fall to roughly 60% of the boutique at a healthy margin. The USAO's 45-90 day resolution pattern means one litigator can carry 60-100 live files, so the constraint on a litigation shop is intake, not lawyer time. Solos are overloaded and fear being first to file. The research found no co-counsel or referral program for other lawyers, so the economics of referral are unexploited.
revenue_model: Client pays $2,995 flat (court costs about $455 passed through). Referral share $900. Illustrative unit economics (assumptions): about $300 paralegal and attorney time, $40 service, about $225 expected tail (15% of cases x roughly $1,500 of MTD opposition work), $60 support, leaving about $1,450 contribution per case. 3,000 cases a year (a year-3 target that requires expanding the market, since the RECAP sample shows only 350-480 filings a year) would produce about $4.3M contribution. Upside: license the ledger, sell overflow capacity to boutiques, and reuse the same referral rails for other agency-delay claims (consular administrative processing, FOIA, passports).
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not tooling but willingness to be counsel of record. Solos already own client trust and stuck files but earn nothing from referring out and fear the suit; a fee share for zero litigation risk turns them from prospects who must be persuaded to pay into an eager, unpaid-acquisition channel, at 30% of fee versus the boutique's SEO and ad spend. Because most cases moot in weeks, the bench recycles capacity fast, and it is the bench, not a tool, that naturally accumulates the full-cycle data (service date, USCIS action date, fee outcome) that makes the ledger better than anyone's public docket analytics. Scale economies and a referral network are both reachable within 24 months.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: get an ethics-counsel memo for NY, NJ and CT on joint-responsibility fee division and a flat-fee MSO; secure a lawyer cofounder or contract litigator admitted in E.D.N.Y., S.D.N.Y., D.N.J. and D. Conn. (the Mandamus.com boutique, admitted in D. Conn., D.D.C. and S.D. Tex., is a possible bench partner rather than only a rival); draft the referral agreement and client consent. Days 10-30: recruit 15 NY/NJ/CT solos through AILA chapters and direct outreach to attorneys of record on RECAP naturalization suits, pre-load 30 stuck cases from their own books, file the first 10 within 72 hours of consent, log every outcome, and pay the first referral share when the client pays. Go/no-go: 10 cases filed, more than half of referrers sending a second case, and modeled contribution of at least $1,000 per case.
lineage: mutation of I1062 ('Delay-Suit Rails for Stuck Immigration Cases'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Bertollini / Mandamus.com (immigration mandamus boutique), Docketwise (immigration case-management software), Alma (tryalma.com, immigration law firm plus tech), Boundless (consumer immigration services). White space: Important caveat first. The WebSearch budget was already spent (200 of 200) before I started, so I ran no web searches at all. I used direct fetches of guessed or known URLs, CourtListener's API and GitHub search. This means 'no direct software competitor found' is weaker evidence than normal. One attempt to load a Google results page returned nothing and was not used. Before committing, someone should run 6-8 real searches (for example 'mandamus AI immigration', 'delay lawsuit software immigration attorneys', Crunchbase, YC, and the AILA and AIC toolkits).

What I found: no software or platform that sells attorney-signed, white-label mandamus filing plus a per-district rules library plus outcome analytics to solo immigration lawyers. The only direct-service players are boutique law firms selling the suit to end clients. Mandamus.com does this at $5,000 plus $500 and gives away templates, and the practice-management incumbent Docketwise has no such feature. The open data (CourtListener) and free guides make the raw ingredients cheap for anyone.

The genuinely unserved wedge is narrow. It is a pre-filing 'will this get mooted or dismissed here' triage, based on real district-by-form-type outcome data, plus a ready-to-file pack for routine delays in the districts where the government usually adjudicates rather than litigates (per Mandamus.com's own data: EDNY, D. Conn., DNJ and EDMI at 83-85% voluntary dismissal after agency action).

Parts of the pitch look weak against what I found:
(1) Nationality-hold suits look poor. Per Mandamus.com's summary of 13 D.D.C. delay decisions from June to August 2026, the government won all 13. Judge Leon in the consolidated Ivanov case found the categorical pause unexplained but dismissed the delay and mandamus counts under TRAC and limited relief to named plaintiffs. A 'nationality hold' template is a liability, not a hook.
(2) S.D. Tex., one of the five launch districts, is hostile. Cheejati v. Blinken (5th Cir. 2024) bars I-485 delay claims on jurisdictional grounds, and DOJ there files motions to dismiss rather than negotiate.
(3) Buckhannon: when USCIS simply adjudicates, the plaintiff is not a prevailing party and can't recover EAJA fees (typically $4,000-$12,000 only if a consent order is obtained). The flat fee holds up, but the 'forced deadline' product should be structured around consent orders.
(4) The '6-10 hour learning curve' is being eroded by free content and general AI drafting.
(5) The data moat is thin. CourtListener docket data is free, and the boutique firms already publish their own district stats. | How this version avoids them: Mandamus.com is a capacity-limited boutique acquiring clients by SEO at $5,000 and shows no co-counsel program; this acquires clients through lawyers who already hold them, prices at about 60% of the boutique, and can even contract the boutique's attorney as bench capacity. Docketwise has no litigation feature and is the natural place for a 'refer this case' button, so it is a channel, not a rival.
